title: Air Traffic Control Systems Are Outdated. What’s Being Done to Prevent Another Outage?
content:
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy on Saturday blamed the previous day’s nationwide ground stop on the replacement of copper wires at a “remote” Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) facility. Installing new fiber optic lines led to critical communication breakdowns, he said.

About 7,500 flights were delayed and over 9,000 were canceled on Friday, according to FlightAware. Some 1.5 million passengers were scheduled to take off from airports in the U.S. after 4 p.m. Eastern, shortly after the ground stop began.

The incident raised questions about what might have led to the historic event—only the second nationwide ground stop since 9/11—and what authorities were doing to prevent it from happening again.

“What we’re working to determine is whether we had incompetence or did they install a faulty router,” Duffy said Saturday, which saw nearly 6,000 additional flights canceled.

As investigators continued working to pinpoint the source of the problem, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford told reporters in Washington, D.C., that disrupted flight schedules were expected to return to normal by the end of Sunday and promised that the “worst is behind us.”

While that may be true for this specific outage, Duffy warned Friday that what happened was not an isolated incident and said that outages would likely continue to occur until antiquated communications equipment across the FAA’s air traffic control network was brought up to date.

“It was the old legacy equipment. It failed,” Duffy said. “And listen, it’s going to continue to fail.”

The Transportation Secretary went on to call for Congress to provide $50 billion before the end of the year to upgrade air traffic control and airport infrastructure, increasing the administration’s recent $30.1 billion request, which included $10.1 billion specifically for air traffic control modernization.

There is reason to believe, however, that financial support alone will not solve the problems currently faced by the FAA. Those include shortages in fully certified air traffic controllers, weaknesses in planning and coordinating necessary modernization work, and vulnerabilities to cybersecurity threats. 

TIME has reached out to Duffy’s office for comment.

Modernizing the FAA’s air traffic control system has been a goal of the industry for years, says Edward Booth, an aviation attorney and pilot based in Jacksonville, and billions of dollars have already been sunk into the process.

“There has been a very methodical four-part, four-stage plan to upgrade that,” Booth tells TIME, referencing NextGen, a multibillion-dollar FAA modernization initiative dating to 2003. It has included shifting toward satellite-based aircraft tracking, digital communications, and more efficient flight routes. 

Booth says a major focus of those earlier modernization efforts was making more efficient use of airspace.

“They have tried to squeeze more airplanes into limited space, make better use of the limited runways available in the system, and they started with completely changing the way airplanes are tracked in the world. It's a world standard now,” he says, pointing to how NextGen has already made strides in air travel.

The agency’s newer overhaul builds on earlier modernization work and includes replacing aging communications equipment, radar, and other infrastructure, with its first phase targeted for completion by the end of 2028.

“It's a very highly technical, robust system,” Booth says of the National Airspace System (NAS), “but it seems the weak spot was discovered yesterday afternoon.”

What’s been done to modernize air traffic control—and what remains?

For more than two decades, the FAA has been working to modernize the NAS while fighting an uphill battle against aging infrastructure. The average U.S. air traffic control tower was 40 years old, and most radar systems were approaching that age, House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee Chairman Sam Graves wrote in a May 2025 op-ed.

Congress had already ordered an independent review of the FAA’s aging technology: The FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 required an audit of legacy systems deployed before 2000—including their vulnerability to single-point failures—and a plan to accelerate replacement or improvement of those found to pose risks. In a written response to Congress, the FAA said that nonprofit research organization MITRE completed the audit in August 2025. The response said the findings would guide modernization efforts, but did not disclose the specific findings or resulting actions.

In July 2025, Congress approved $12.5 billion for the FAA to upgrade its “radar, software, hardware, and telecommunications” at more than 4,600 sites through December 2028. 

As of Nov. 5, the FAA said it has “replaced 69% of copper wires, installed Surface Awareness Initiative (SAI) systems at 143 towers, transitioned 26 towers to electronic flight strips [and] installed 226 IP Voice Switches.”

The updates were noted within an announcement saying the FAA was beginning to phase out the floppy disks used in air traffic control. It said that it had launched a replacement system that would include a digital display board with data about disruptions, weather conditions, and advisories. The announcement identified five initial facilities and set a goal of installing the system at 435 sites by the end of 2028.

Duffy called these efforts “the latest signal that America’s brand new air traffic control system is coming at lightning speed.”

The FAA then announced Nov. 10 that it was expanding its AI-powered scheduling and flight-planning tool—known as SMART (Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes, and Trajectories)—to airspace managed by all 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers nationwide. SMART is part of a 12-year, $875 million contract that also covers the agency’s Flow Management Data and Services program.

Duffy said at Friday’s press conference that SMART had nothing to do with the disruption.

Why can one equipment failure cause widespread disruption?

Describing Friday's outage, Duffy said a router being replaced as workers switched from copper wiring to fiber-optic connections began flooding other routers with more than 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, disrupting communications and some radar feeds. Systems came back online after officials isolated the work at the remote location, he said.

For Booth, the spread of that disruption underscores the need for safeguards that can contain a problem in one part of the FAA’s communications network before it affects the wider system.

“They need a system that is not prone to single-point failures,” he says.

Booth pointed out that legacy systems—often relying on analog lines, decades-old routers, and interconnected regional hubs—lack the fault-tolerant design needed to prevent a local or routine maintenance glitch from cascading nationwide.

“The public probably would be shocked to learn that the way pilots communicate with air traffic control is tantamount to an old-fashioned telephone line,” he says. “You've got 10, sometimes 15 airplanes competing to talk to a single controller-specified frequency.”

Kumar Sokka, the CEO of Acre Security, says a key consideration when upgrading complex systems is whether individual components can fail without disrupting the entire network.

“Can you remove a single point of failure? Are these systems distributed in a way where it's siloed in certain structures where if something fails, not everything fails, right?” asks Sokka.

He says that many industries come up against issues of balancing the high upfront expense of upgrading legacy systems against the severe financial and operational risks of future outages. 

Companies can overhaul different parts of their systems at different times, he says.

“You can do it over time and not necessarily everything at once,” Sokka says. “You can get your software and the data modernized first so you can do preventative work of monitoring the health of a system constantly. And then over time, you can change out the hardware, because that’s the most expensive part.”

Integrating new technology with older equipment presents its own challenges. At Friday’s briefing, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said new equipment had overwhelmed the older system, although the precise cause remained under investigation. “Nickel and diming it together does not work. This is what happens when that takes place,” he said.

Duffy said that the FAA is working to get the travel ecosystem back on track in time for Thanksgiving, which is one of the busiest travel periods of the year in the U.S. According to Airlines for America, nearly 29 million passengers are expected to travel by plane between Nov. 20 and Nov. 30.

title: The China Shock in the AI Era
content:
Americans are anxious about artificial intelligence. In the midterm elections, they voted to slow down its expansion. Forty local ballot measures in 10 states promise to tighten restrictions on data-center construction, with overwhelming public support. Measures to limit development of data centers won more than 70% of the vote in 30 of these electoral contests. A 2026 survey by Pew Research Center found that about 52% of Americans were more concerned than excited about the growing use of AI in daily life, up from 37% in 2021. Only 9% were more excited than concerned, and roughly six in ten said they wanted more control over how AI is used in their lives.

The sources of anxiety about AI are many: the safety of increasingly powerful systems and the ability to control them; the fear of job displacement; surveillance and the loss of privacy; a rising tide of misinformation and deep fakes; the enormous amounts of electricity and water that the data centers consume; and the concentration of wealth and power in a handful of companies that own the frontier AI models.

And there is geopolitics.

Until now, anxiety about the role of AI in geopolitical competition has largely been confined to policy circles. But the possibility that Jensen Huang, who resigned as chief executive of Nvidia on Thursday, may have been compromised in a potential espionage scandal has brought that anxiety into the broader public sphere, fueling a frenzy over AI and the competition between the United States and China.  

China is at the center of arguably two of the world’s most consequential economic and political developments: its dominance in global trade and its formidable AI capabilities. China and America are AI superpowers, but their strengths differ. America leads in computing power, thanks largely to Nvidia’s advanced chips. China is catching up fast in AI models. The economic and geopolitical implications of this competition are enormous.

There is another dimension to this competition: the economic effects of China’s trade dominance and the rising role of AI in the economy could reinforce each other and produce greater impact than either would have alone. China’s trade dominance is well-known. Two decades earlier, the economists David H. Autor, David Dorn, and Gordon H. Hanson gave that anxiety a name when they coined the term “China Shock” to describe the impact of the massive increase in Chinese exports to the U.S. in the early 2000s. The surge contributed to a sharp decline in American manufacturing and the loss of more than two million jobs in certain regions of the United States. Over the past two decades, the so-called China Shock has gone global, as Chinese exports have surged around the world without a comparable rise in China’s imports.

The world may soon experience the convergence of two enormous economic shocks, each reinforcing the other in terms of their direction and magnitude: The China Shock and the AI Productivity Shock. The consequences of AI-driven productivity growth remain contested. But the fear is that AI will enable companies to dramatically increase output without employing more people or raising the income of ordinary citizens. The China Shock has a similar effect. China has become a dominant force in advanced manufacturing in electric vehicles, batteries, solar panels, artificial intelligence, and robotic technology. But China’s growing competitiveness has led to a global surge of Chinese exports without a corresponding global surge of Chinese imports.

On top of the China Shock, the AI Productivity Shock could further widen the gap between global supply and demand, and create new economic imbalances and strains on a scale the world has not witnessed. 

The coming AI productivity shock 

The China Shock and the AI Productivity Shock share one critical feature: both can produce a glut of output without generating a corresponding increase in demand. In China, production has grown faster than consumption; with AI, the fear is that the technology will generate wealth without creating jobs. In both cases, the gains tend to flow to the owners of capital—and in China’s case, also to the government—rather than to workers and households.

But the iron law of economics still holds: supply requires demand, and an economy can absorb a large increase in output only if enough people have the income to buy what it produces. Economists have long described it as a problem of effective demand: the recognition that supply does not automatically create its own demand. For that to happen, greater production and supply have to translate into more jobs and higher incomes.

Whether AI will create such an imbalance is still a matter of debate. Optimists point to earlier waves of automation. Technologies such as the tractor and the spreadsheet displaced certain kinds of work but eventually helped create other kinds of work and generated jobs and additional income for workers. Only time will tell whether AI, which differs significantly from earlier technologies, will follow that pattern. What we do know is that this optimistic scenario of technological progress has yet to deliver the gains in employment and household purchasing power in China.

China is now regarded as one of the world’s leading technological powers. In some industries, China’s factories are producing more than the global demand put together. China makes more than 80% of the world’s solar panels, and its factories can turn out roughly twice as many modules in a year as the entire planet installs. In batteries, China’s manufacturing capacity is already more than double the current global demand. One projection suggests that, by 2030, China alone could produce more batteries than the whole world will use.

But China’s technological advancement is far more visible in what its factories can produce than in what its households can afford to buy and consume. Youth unemployment in the country is rising, and domestic consumption has stagnated. The unemployment rate among urban Chinese aged 16 to 24 climbed to a record 18.9 % in August 2025, according to official statistics. The real figure is likely to be much higher.

Economic progress is defined by progress in both production and consumption. These two areas of human activity move in tandem with each other and are mutually reinforcing. Faster productivity leads to rising output, which raises incomes and allows households to buy more of what is being produced. Historically, before the age of AI, this has been the case. The China Shock and the AI Productivity Shock may break that connection. What made, and continues to make, the China Shock so disruptive is the immense disparity between the scale of China’s exports and its purchases from the rest of the world. China’s imports consist largely of agricultural products, minerals, and energy products that it cannot produce in sufficient quantities on its soil.

China’s exports lower prices for consumers abroad, a benefit on the expenditure side. But households need income to consume, and that income comes from the production side of the economy. But the Chinese economy is not generating a corresponding increase in income for the rest of the world by importing more from them and boosting their production. China has roughly 35% of the world’s manufacturing capacity but accounts for about just 11% of global consumption. Household consumption in the country amounts to a mere 39% of its GDP, compared with 68% in America. This imbalance is unsustainable—for both China and the world.

Low domestic consumption forces Chinese businesses to sell more abroad, often at cutthroat prices. Cheaper imports benefit consumers abroad, but when local companies close or cut jobs, workers lose income and can no longer afford to buy as much, including goods from China. In the long run, the China Shock poses a risk to China itself. The more efficacious China is at expanding production under these conditions, the more it risks undermining demand for its products in the future. There is very little benefit to the Chinese economy if businesses fail and unemployment rises in the rest of the world.

Taken too far, one-sided trade eventually backfires on the country that benefits from it today. The strains are already visible across the developing world. The economists Shoumitro Chatterjee and Arvind Subramanian argue that the “real casualties” of a new China Shock will be low-and middle-income countries, where hundreds of millions of people still depend on manufacturing for jobs and upward mobility. From Southeast Asia to Latin America, a flood of cheap Chinese goods has begun to shutter local factories and provoke a wave of new tariffs and anti-dumping cases.

The costs of overproduction

China need not have grown its economy this way. Its rapid GDP growth, its impressive technological prowess, and its vast population could have made it a much larger market for goods made at home and abroad. Beijing could have strengthened the social safety net for its citizens, and eased the burden on households of paying for healthcare and saving for retirement. Instead, it has focused singularly on expanding production by offering lavish subsidies to businesses and favoring capital over labor in many of its programs.

For many Chinese families, those burdens are heavy. Chinese households pay roughly a third of the country’s healthcare costs out of their own pockets, a higher share than in most rich countries. State support is particularly meager for the country’s hundreds of millions of rural residents, whose pensions remain minimal. The national minimum basic pension was raised to just 143 yuan a month in 2025, about a dollar a day, while the average rural payout is only around 246 yuan a month, below the World Bank’s poverty standard.

The cumulative result of these policy choices has made Chinese citizens more important to the economy as workers than as consumers, as they produce more than they consume. The signs of this imbalance are staggering. As I have written elsewhere, the share of labor compensation relative to total economic inputs in agriculture, industry, and utilities dropped from 21% in 1987 to 15% in 2023. 

Wages as a share of manufacturing output in China are among the lowest in the world. The ratio of the minimum wage to GDP per capita fell from 0.37 in 2000 to 0.27 in 2024, leaving China’s statutory monthly minimum wage below that of lower-income neighbors such as Vietn

The relative slide in income growth amid rapid GDP growth is rooted in the Chinese economic system. So far, the full effects of AI and robotic technology on employment and incomes of Chinese citizens have yet to be fully registered. Given how fast these technologies are progressing, their combined effect could compound existing imbalances within years rather than decades.

The fierce competition among Chinese companies to sell more than their home market can absorb is already sending shock waves through the global economy. As AI and robotics would allow these companies to produce still more without a corresponding increase in jobs or wages, the two shocks will reinforce and amplify each other. The world is ill-prepared for the combined impact of the China Shock and the AI Productivity Shock.

For China, the wise course of action is to focus on the income side of its economy, beginning with reducing the inequities between rural and urban citizens and spending more on people rather than on buildings and machinery. For the West, it is prudent to rethink how to share the gains from AI in economies where most people depend on a watertight relationship between work and compensation.  

China’s factories and AI technology can generate abundance. Whether that abundance translates into greater common welfare and sustains long-term growth is the big question. Policymakers in China and the West need to act now and work together to turn greater productive capacity into shared prosperity

title: Congress Must Protect the CDC From Politics
content:
Democrats and Republicans in the new Congress will disagree about plenty in health policy. However, they should agree that the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) should be a scientific agency whose judgments hold steady no matter who occupies the White House. In January, Congress will have the chance to write that principle into law.

For decades, the scientific independence of America’s public health agencies rested on a bipartisan understanding. Presidential administrations disagreed about health policy, sometimes profoundly, but their health secretaries generally respected the expertise and established processes of agencies like the CDC and the Food and Drug Administration.

Earlier administrations of both parties—including those of Republican Secretary of Health and Human Services Alex Azar and Democratic Secretary Xavier Becerra—faced charges of political interference, particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic, and some had merit. But I would argue that none have even approached the scale and scope of Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s interventions. The safeguards that existed were administrative policies, and a new secretary can discard them.

In June 2025, Kennedy dismissed all 17 members of the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices and replaced them with his own appointees. No prior secretary had done this. Congress had given U.S. Health and Human Services secretaries broad authority and relied on their restraint. Restraint is a tradition, and the past year shows it can end.

To address this, Congress should pursue four priorities.

First, write scientific independence into law

Elected leaders have a legitimate role in setting national health priorities and holding agencies accountable. That role ends where scientific judgment begins, and Congress should draw the line in statute:

  • Codify the advisory committee on immunization with clear membership qualifications, a transparent appointment process, and removal only for cause.

  • Require documented, public evidence reviews behind any major change to a scientific recommendation.

  • Require a secretary who departs from a formal recommendation to explain why in public, separating the scientific evidence from considerations like cost and implementation.

  • Protect career scientists’ ability to publish findings and communicate evidence, and create an independent office to investigate political interference, with whistleblower protections.

These rules must bind every future secretary, including those appointed by the party that controls Congress today. A protection that works against only one party’s appointees will not last.

Rebuild the CDC’s workforce and expertise

The CDC has lost more than a quarter of its workforce since 2024. The losses include epidemiologists who investigate outbreaks, laboratory scientists who identify emerging pathogens, specialists who evaluate evidence, and professionals who work with state and local health departments. That expertise takes years to develop.

Congress should require an independent assessment of the CDC’s current capabilities and direct the agency to produce a public rebuilding plan with measurable targets for restoring essential functions. Personnel protections should support a professional scientific workforce that can serve administrations of either party. Targets should follow the agency’s mission, whatever headcount that implies.

Write the CDC’s core responsibilities into law, starting with data

COVID exposed confusion about the separate roles of the federal and state governments. The CDC could issue guidance, but implementation depended on state and local officials working under different laws, budgets, and political pressures.

Congress should specify what Americans can count on their national public health agency to do: investigate outbreaks when states request help, publish evidence-based guidance, and operate a national data system that state and local health departments can contribute to and draw from in near real time. It should fund those partners to participate, because the CDC’s guidance reaches Americans through their local health departments.

Pair independence with accountability

Scientific independence invites scrutiny, and protecting the CDC from political interference makes meaningful accountability more important. Congress should establish public measures of performance. 

How effectively does the CDC identify and investigate emerging threats? How quickly does it get reliable information to states? How transparently does it evaluate evidence? How well does it communicate uncertainty and update recommendations as evidence changes?

An independent body should evaluate these questions, accounting for outcomes that depend on state and local partners. The purpose is to find weaknesses and improve performance.

With a Republican president in the White House, sweeping legislation will require bipartisan support. Congress can begin with oversight hearings, appropriations language, and independent investigations while it builds a coalition for lasting statutory protections. And they can start by pursuing common-sense, common-ground policies. 

For eight decades, the CDC has protected Americans from infectious diseases and other health threats. Americans deserve a CDC whose science they can trust, whose expertise is protected, and whose ability to safeguard their health does not depend on who occupies the White House.

title: How to Check Your Flight Status After the FAA Canceled the Ground Stop for All Airports
content:
Update, 8:41 p.m.: The Federal Aviation Administration announced it has ended the ground stop.

On Friday afternoon, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ordered a nationwide ground stop for all airports in the United States. If you're planning to fly this afternoon or evening, or you have friends or family doing the same, you're likely concerned about tracking flight statuses. While there's still a lot we don't know, there are tools to help track flights at this time:

How to track flights during the nationwide ground stop

There are a number of options for tracking flights, whether you have your flight number or not. If you have the flight number, the fastest method is to Google it: Google will display a live tracker of your flight at the top of the results page. You can also head to the airline's official website to track your flight: United Airlines, for example, has a flight tracker where you can either enter your route information or your flight number. Most, if not all, airlines will have a similar tool you can use.

Alternatively, you can use a site or service that tracks all flights. FlightAware is one such site and has a flight tracker that lets you search flights—so long as you know the origin and the destination. If you have the flight number, your iPhone can help: You can enter your flight number into Spotlight search to see a live tracker, or you can text a contact your flight number, then tap the link that appears under the number to see a tracker of the flight.

Why did the FAA order a nationwide ground stop?

At this time, the exact reason isn't totally clear. According to the agency, “The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following communication issues impacting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers,” but the FAA hasn't said what caused those communications issues or when they expect to lift the grounding. The grounding order comes one day after a massive Microsoft outage that disrupted service for users of Outlook, Teams, and other Microsoft products. It also comes one day after Ars Technica reported that the FAA was rolling out an AI-powered tool to help manage air traffic across the country.

This is only the third time in U.S. history that the FAA has made such an order—once after 9/11, and again in January of 2023 due to a pilot alert system issue; the latter ground stop lasted around 90 minutes.

title: I Analyzed the Seven Biggest AI Chatbots to Determine How Safe They Are for Kids
content:
AI safety for both adults and children is under greater scrutiny than ever before, with a growing number of questions and concerns appearing around how beneficial or otherwise these conversational bots actually are for our mental well-being—even without considering their energy use, ethics, or economic implications. At the same time, an increasing number of apps and services are becoming age-gated in a growing number of countries around the world, as governments realize that letting kids loose on AI apps, social media platforms, and the web at large might not be the best idea for their ongoing development and prosperity.

The big AI apps, such as ChatGPT and Gemini, are right in the center of these trends, and the companies behind them are taking steps that they promise will keep children safe. If you want to know what youngsters in your family may be getting exposed to, and what you can do about it, here's the rundown.

ChatGPT

OpenAI's ChatGPT has one of the more comprehensive setups in terms of parental controls. The minimum age for users is 13, and if you're under 18, you need to have parental consent to open an account—age is predicted via several signals, including what times of day you use ChatGPT and what you talk about.

Accounts for under-18s automatically become ChatGPT for Teens accounts. There's more of a focus on learning and study (with a dedicated study mode), as well as "age-appropriate safeguards to help reduce exposure to sensitive or potentially harmful content." There are built-in protections for "harmful topics," including sexual, romantic, or violent roleplay, graphic violence, and self-harm. These work on top of the safeguards for all users that limit chats about physical harm and illegal activity.

These ChatGPT for Teens accounts can also be linked to a parental account—but while parental consent is required for under-18s to use the service, ChatGPT clearly says that teens do have the option to break the link if they want. If you do persuade your kid to keep your accounts connected, you can set time limits on when the AI bot can be used, and tweak some of the sensitivity settings. However, you can't view any conversations.

To set up parental controls from ChatGPT on the web, click your profile icon (bottom left), then Settings > Parental controls > Add family member and follow the instructions. It's also worth bearing in mind that ChatGPT app can also be used for free, anonymously, in any web browser, though OpenAI says users accessing the AI this way are subject to the default under-18s limits (and can't save chats or access an archive).

Gemini

Gemini is tied into everything else Google does, and follows the broader rules for Google accounts: No under-13s, unless you're part of a family group and using an account managed by an adult. You can manage your family through the Family Link portal on the web, though as far as parental controls specific to Gemini go, you can only enable or disable access to the AI (settings like screen time apply across all enabled apps).

For all under-18s (partly identified through age estimation), whether or not they're part of a managed family group, Google applies some additional protections. They include preventing the AI from taking on a persona, guarding against emotional dependence on the AI, and discouraging bullying and other forms of harassment. There are also safeguards to limit chats about age-restricted substances like alcohol or vapes, and mental health issues like eating disorders.

These protections for minors are applied in addition to the usual guardrails in Gemini for everyone. The guardrails should lead you away from conversations about self-harm, suicide, violence, and illegal activities, and offer quick links to support in times of crisis. However, Google itself admits that these filters aren't perfect.

As with ChatGPT, there's a loophole of sorts in that anyone can start chatting with Gemini, for free inside a web browser, with no checks at all. These conversations can't be saved and come up against usage limits fairly quickly, but they're only protected by the general restrictions for all accounts, not the ones specific to minors.

Google has ways of telling if you're lying about your age. Credit: Lifehacker

Meta AI

Meta AI will show up in several apps that young people and children are likely to use, including WhatsApp and Instagram, as well as having its own separate app on the web and on phones. The standard restrictions for Meta's social media accounts apply to its AI too: A minimum age of 13, and restrictions for all under-18s. Like many other platforms, it uses some AI magic to flag up accounts being used by minors.

If you're under 18 and on a Meta Teen account, you'll come up against blocks if you try to get Meta AI to engage in sexual or romantic roleplay, or discuss alcohol or substance misuse. Chats on topics such as eating disorders and self-harm will prompt the AI to offer guidance towards relevant support services.

Meta offers a comprehensive parental control setup for its apps, including Meta AI, but connecting a parent account isn't compulsory for teens. This is handled through the Meta Family Center portal, and parents can get reports on the general topics that kids are chatting about with AI—though they don't get the exact transcripts or prompts. Any self-harm or suicide discussion can trigger an alert to the connected parent account.

All users, under 18 or over 18, get support and crisis intervention responses when chatting about suicide and self-harm, and there are strict limits on discussing illegal and harmful acts, including drug use and cyberbullying, as well as sexual and adult content.

Siri AI

Apple users have to be 13 or over to have an account, which is required to access Siri AI—anyone younger needs to have an account created for them by an adult, and these accounts can only get at the basic, older Siri. Date of birth must be declared when opening an Apple account, with tighter checks rolling out in many parts of the world.

Anyone over the age of 13 can have an Apple account and use the Siri AI app, with or without a connected parent account, as it stands in most U.S. states. This means the well-being safeguards are essentially the same for teens as they are for adults: There are safeguards around self-harm, suicide, sexual and violent content, and illegal commands. It's one of the more conservative AIs when it comes to what it will talk about.

The new and improved Siri AI can be managed to some extent by the new parental controls available in iOS 27 and Apple's other software updates for 2026—Apple has clearly seen the way the wind is blowing—but this is optional for teens. It depends on whether or not you can corral your kids into a Family Sharing group.

If your teens are in your family group of users, then the standard Screen Time rules apply for controlling app usage limits and device access (in iOS Settings, tap your name, then Family to get at them). There are also options for disabling certain Siri AI features, such as the writing tools or the image creation capabilities.

Copilot

Like Gemini/Google and Apple/Siri, Copilot is tied into the wider Microsoft ecosystem, and access for under-18s can be managed through it. Users must be 13 or older to hold a Microsoft or a Copilot account—and again, there's some underlying tech in place to detect anyone who might be deliberately lying about their age.

If you've got a teen using Copilot, you can manage their access through the standard Microsoft Family Safety portal. You're able to enable or disable Copilot access, set times during which Copilot can and can't be used, and disable certain features like image generation or voice mode. Parents can't read the Copilot chats of their kids, though.

Parental supervision is optional—a teen aged 13–17 can use Copilot without linking their account to an adult one. Microsoft says users identified as under 18 won't see personalized results or ads, and will get age-appropriate responses regarding risky or harmful content, though there's not much detail on what that entails.

More generally, content around self-harm, violence, adult content, harassment, and harmful or illegal activity is banned on the AI platform. Any prompts about suicide or drugs will bring up support options rather than answers, whether you're an adult or a young person using the service.

Copilot can no longer be accessed anonymously on the web—you need an account. Credit: Lifehacker

Grok

Out of the bigger AI chatbots out there, Grok is very much the worst at protecting minors. It can be accessed through X or as its own standalone app, and while its terms of use indicate there's a minimum age requirement of 13, a recent report by Common Sense Media says the platform's age checks aren't effective.

Ultimately that means that minors have the same access to Grok as adults, if they want it—an AI platform that combines "weak safety guardrails" and "a range of extremely harmful content" that includes "explicit sexual content, mental health risks, violent content, and inappropriate responses to... offensive content" (that's the Common Sense Media Report again).

Yes, this is the AI chatbot that has previously had a problem with deepfake porn imagery, and which has traditionally taken a rather casual attitude towards safety concerns, led by SpaceXAI CEO Elon Musk. While illegal and harmful content is supposedly banned from Grok, its own FAQs admit that certain chats can result in "dialogue that may involve coarse language, crude humor, sexual situations, or violence."

There is actually a Grok Kids Mode that limits the kind of content that can be shown and the conversation topics that can be added, but it requires users to self-declare themselves as minors and is easy to bypass. The advice from Common Sense Media seems to be the way to go with Grok: Do not let your teens access it.

Claude

Claude's approach to child safety is straightforward: You can only register for an account if you're over 18. It is possible to lie about your age when signing up, but like the other platforms, Anthropic looks at various "signals" in behavior to spot minors—if your account gets flagged, you have to verify your age using an option like face age estimation or Yoti.

There's no free web access to the chatbot, like there is with ChatGPT and Gemini, so if you're under 18, you're locked out from the service unless you know the behavioral tricks to get past Claude's detection systems.

In terms of more general well-being protections on Claude, any chat around self-harm or suicide will guide users towards helplines and other resources for support. Conversations about illegal activities, disallowed speech, and explicit sexual content are banned from the platform. In recent months, Anthropic says it's also reduced AI sycophancy.

That's something of a whistle-stop tour of the big seven AI chatbots, but if you're a parent, it should give you some idea of what's out there and how easy it is to access. Besides the parental controls built into these AIs (or not), you also have the settings available at the platform level—Android, iOS, Windows, macOS—to restrict the use of any potentially harmful apps.

title: Fatih Birol: The Energy World Will Never Be the Same As Before the Iran War
content:
For more than a decade, Fatih Birol has been one of the world’s most influential voices in energy markets. As the head of the International Energy Agency (IEA), he advises presidents and energy ministers; CEOs follow his view of the market with careful attention.   

When we caught up at the United Nations climate change conference, known as COP31, currently underway in Antalya, Turkey, he offered a blunt analysis: the war in Iran has unleashed a structural shift. "I don't see any credible pathway in which the world of energy is going back where it was before the Iran War," he said on Nov. 13. 

A quick analysis might boil this shift down to simple terms. In general, the focus on energy security will mean more renewable energy because it can be produced locally. It will mean efficiency measures so that countries use less fuel and are less vulnerable to shocks. Indeed, an energy crisis policy tracker from the IEA cites dozens of policies countries have laid out this year to do just that—from a push for biodiesel in Indonesia to incentives for consumers to install solar and storage in Bangladesh. 

But Birol says the coming structural changes in energy will have even wider implications, shaping economic and geopolitical outcomes. He cites economic diversification plans from oil-exporting countries, new trade partnerships, and investments in new technologies like next-generation batteries and nuclear power. All of which comes with an eye toward safeguarding energy supply from supply disruptions. "Instead of importing energy, they are deciding to build energy,” he told me. 

A key theme in Antalya—and on Birol’s mind—is electrification. Right now less than a quarter of final energy consumption comes from electricity. The rest comes primarily from fuel consumption, think of petrol in vehicles, heating oil in homes, or gas in stoves. Relying on electricity, which tends to be produced relatively close to where it’s used, addresses energy security concerns. That’s even more the case when electricity is produced using renewables rather than imported fossil fuels. 

The COP31 presidency is pushing countries to pledge to rely on electricity for 35% of their final energy consumption by 2035. The world’s electricity grid still relies on fossil fuels to some degree—more or less so depending on the area—but today it’s typically cleaner than most fossil fuels. It will be even cleaner as renewable deployment continues. 

Electrification also represents a structural shift. It promises to reshape trade relationships as countries need to either build clean technology supply chains or identify friendly partners to build relevant trade relationships. It will spur investment in the power sector, advancing both big electric infrastructure projects and creating new companies that build innovative electricity technologies. In the IEA’s special report on electrification released in September, the agency says that annual global investment in electricity generation, battery storage, and grids could total $2.5 trillion by 2035 in a scenario where electrification really takes off. That’s a $1 trillion increase from last year. And electrification promises to unlock—or at least lessen—the stranglehold that oil and gas has on geopolitics while elevating the importance of another set of resources, including critical minerals. 

“Two years ago, I said we are entering the age of electricity,” Birol told me. “I can tell you today, when I look at today's numbers, we are in the age of electricity."

title: 10 Hacks Every watchOS 27 User Should Know
content:
watchOS 27 introduces a solid set of upgrades to your wrist—assuming your Apple Watch supports it. While the newest update isn't Apple's most feature-filled, it does include a number of changes that improve the way you exercise, track your health, and locate missing items. That's especially true for anyone with the latest Series 12 or Ultra 4. If your Apple Watch supports watchOS 27, you should know about these 10 hacks:

Use this hidden gesture to find the app switcher

With watchOS 27, Apple changed what double-pressing the Digital Crown does. Instead of opening the app switcher, it now triggers Audio Intelligence—if you have an Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4. If you don't have access to those features, the gesture now does nothing.

It seems Apple realized the mistake, however, as evidenced by watchOS 27.2. When you're using an app while running this latest update, press and hold the bottom part of the watch's screen, and you'll trigger the app switcher. You can now jump to a different app, or close an app that isn't working. Sadly, this only works when you're already in an app, and not when you're on the Home Screen, but it's certainly better than nothing.

Add suggested widgets to the Home Screen using the Siri Modular Watch Face

Credit: Khamosh Pathak

While you can load up multiple complications on your Apple Watch, they aren't exactly dynamic. That's why I'm a big fan of the Smart Stack widgets on the Apple Watch, which update dynamically to show contextual information. Now, with the new Siri Modular Face, you can access dynamic widgets on the Home Screen. If you've just parked your car, for example, you'll see a widget showing its location; likewise, if you have an upcoming calendar appointment, it will be front and center.

To use the Siri Modular watch face, tap and hold on the screen, go to the end of the list, tap the Plus button, and find and add the Siri Modular watch face. Once you do, you'll start seeing dynamic widgets when you wake up your watch. Don't expect much personalization from this watch face, however. You can customize the colors and add three small complications, but that's it.

Use the new single-tap gesture to open apps and perform actions

The double-tap gesture is one of my favorite Apple Watch features. By tapping your thumb and index finger together twice, you can do things like answer a call or reply to a message. In watchOS 27, Apple took the gesture one step forward. You can now use the double-tap gesture to scroll through your widgets; if you perform a single tap, it then opens the highlighted widget or the shortcut. This means you can open and browse the weather app, or start a workout, without ever touching your Apple Watch's screen.

Use Shazam to identify songs even when you're offline

Credit: Khamosh Pathak

Your Apple Watch's new Music Recognition app has native Shazam integration. What's more, Shazam will record your request even when you're offline and away from your iPhone. The moment you reconnect, the service will identify the songs, which you can see in the Shazam app on your iPhone or Apple Watch.

It seems like Apple has a library of songs it uses for offline recognition, because in my testing, it was able to recognize a Coldplay song instantly, even when in Airplane mode. To use it, you can either open the Music Recognition app, or you can add the widget for faster access. Scroll up on the Home Screen, go to the bottom of the screen, tap the Edit button, then the Plus button, and add the Music Recognition widget.

Use the Step Count widget to get live step count monitoring

Apple Watches have traditionally lacked a live step count widget or complication. To find your step count, you had to go to the bottom of the Activity app, or rely on third-party apps. But even still, these apps never showed live data. You’d always have to wait a couple of seconds to see the updated stats.

Now, if you own the latest Apple Watch Series 12 or the Ultra 4, you can add a live step count widget or complication to the Apple Watch face or the Smart Stack. This will show you your precise step count at all times. To use it, go to the bottom of the Smart Stack, tap the Edit button, then tap the Plus button. Here, find and add the new Step count widget.

Continue Siri AI conversations from your iPhone to your Apple Watch

Credit: Apple

Siri is no longer a voice assistant that you use for one-off tasks. With Siri AI, you can now carry on multiple conversations with context and memory. It's not as robust as ChatGPT or Claude, but you can use Siri AI for brainstorming, researching, and jotting down ideas for later.

The Siri AI app on the iPhone shows all your conversations, and so does the Apple Watch. This means you can continue your Siri AI conversations and view past chats on your Apple Watch. To use it, press the Digital Crown once, then tap the Siri app icon in the center. This will open up all your conversations instead of calling upon Siri. Tap a conversation to continue your chat on the Apple Watch. Of course, anything you do here will be reflected in the Siri app on your iPhone.

Find people and items from the Watch in the new Find My app

Credit: Apple

The new Find My app on the Apple Watch shows a single map for finding people, devices, and items. This means you can now locate your family members who are sharing their location with you, as well as AirTags or other Find My items from the watchOS app.

After opening the app, you can use the Digital Crown to zoom in or out of the map. Use touch to pan around. The map doesn't show all items and people at once, though. Tap the Menu button at the bottom-right corner, and then switch between People, Items, or Devices. If you have multiple items, you can scroll through them using the Digital Crown.

Use the Readiness Score to figure out how much to push yourself

Credit: Apple

While it's not a Whoop-level feature, the Apple Watch now includes a Readiness score. Instead of individually looking at your training load, sleep score, and vitals, you now have one number that gives you the whole picture.

The Readiness score ranges from 0 to 10 and is based on your recent fitness activity, sleep data, and background health monitoring. If you have a score of 8 to 10, your Apple Watch thinks you can push yourself, or "go for it," as it says; if it's below 5, the watch thinks you should consider lighter activity. This feature, though, is only available on Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. You can use the new Readiness app on your Apple Watch to see this data, but you can also access it on your iPhone in the Fitness app's new Readiness section.

Use Max Extended Workout mode to boost your Apple Watch's battery life

Credit: Khamosh Pathak

Low Power Mode isn't your only option when it comes to extending the battery life for your Apple Watch. watchOS 27 offers a special Max Extended Workout mode just for long workouts. With it, your Apple Watch disables some features, like splits and alerts, and reduces the frequency of GPS and heart rate readings, in the hopes of extending your battery throughout your entire exercise. To use it, go to the Workout app and select the workout you want. Tap the Goals button in the top-right corner, and choose the Extended option. Then, switch to the Max Extended option and start your workout.

Use Sound Recognition to get notified about sirens, alarms, and other noises

Credit: Apple

The Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 come with a set of Audio Intelligence features that use the microphones on the Apple Watch, paired with AI models (both local and cloud-based), to identify sounds, music, and record conversation. Thanks to this new feature, one of the iPhone's accessibility features also makes its way to the Apple Watch.

Sound Recognition can alert you when it hears sirens, alarms, doorbells, and more, even when your iPhone isn’t around. To set this up, go to the Settings app on your iPhone and navigate to Accessibility > Sound & Name Recognition > Sound Recognition. Here, enable the sounds you want to monitor, and make sure to turn on the Detect using Apple Watch toggle.

title: Five Hacks Every Apple Watch Series 12 User Should Know
content:
We may earn a commission from links on this page.

The latest Apple Watches have a lot of new features that older watches don't, so I figured it was time for a new list of hacks. While our general Apple Watch and fitness tracking hacks are still golden, Series 12 devices offer new features like native step counting, a Readiness app, an upgraded heart rate sensor, an AI-based version of Siri, and "audio intelligence" that can replay and summarize real-life conversations, within limits. Here's how to get the most out of them.

Apple Watch Series 12
