Put the steps complication on your watch face to turn it into a simple pedometer

The Series 12 can finally count steps natively, a task that for some reason is only arriving now, and is restricted to just the newest Apple Watch models. Enjoy it! To add a step counter to your watch face, long-press on the clock screen to edit it, tap on a complication (that’s what Apple calls those little icons and numbers that appear on some watch faces), choose Activity, and then tap Steps. 

Get better Siri Recaps by turning them off by default

You don’t need this creepy feature listening in to everything, but it can be nice to have it as a backup on occasion. A button in your Apple Watch’s Control Center can turn the feature on and off. Keep it off except when you have a structured conversation that you’ll want to refer to later. This feature is currently in beta (which you can try now if you want to), but is expected to be available to everyone later this year.

It's worth turning off the default setting not just because of the creepiness factor, but also because the recaps work best when there is a single subject of conversation, with a clear start and end, and just one context. If you leave recaps running all the time, your doctor’s appointment will get mixed in with your grocery shopping, YouTube watching, and everyday chatter. 

To finish off a recap and make it useful, take a look at the recap shortly after the conversation, tap the three-dots menu, and hit Edit. You’ll be able to adjust the notes and add your own important details. Siri won’t identify speakers and seems to shy away from including certain details, like people’s names. You can add in what it missed and also create your own bullet points so that everything gets noted down while it’s still fresh in your mind. 

Learn these gestures to access features more easily

This one isn’t specific to the Series 12, but if you haven’t gotten on board with the pinch and wrist flick gestures yet, now is a great time. 

First, the wrist flick: If a notification is on your screen, or you’re otherwise looking at something you’d rather be done with, just flick your wrist away from you and then back toward you, as if there were a crumb on the watch face and you wanted to knock it off. This will bring you back to the watch face and close whatever you were looking at. 

The double pinch is another useful one, although Apple calls it double tap. This is confusing because you aren’t double tapping the watch, you’re tapping your thumb and forefinger together while wearing the watch. You don’t need to touch the watch face at all. So, when you get a notification or a call, look at it on your watch, and pinch your thumb and forefinger (of the watch hand) together twice. The watch detects the pinch from subtle movements in your wrist, and it will open the notification. You can then use the wrist flick to close the notification. Performing a double pinch when no notification is on screen will bring up your smart stack. You can then double-pinch to move to the next card in the smart stack, or single-pinch to open that card and see its details. 

If you want to learn even more gestures, go into the Watch app, and select Accessibility and then Hand gestures. You can remap a whole-fist “clench” to do the same thing as pressing the digital crown, for example, or to open the control center or Siri. 

Slap your watch to make Siri shut up

A little rude, perhaps, but helpful: With the new AI-based Siri, sometimes answers to questions can be long-winded. If Siri launches into a novel-length response and you’re not interested in hearing all that, just put your palm over the screen. You’ll instantly be transported back to your watch face, and the Siri response will stop. 

Turn on Silent responses so you can read what Siri says instead of listening to it

If you still want to see those longer responses without having Siri read the whole thing to you, you can set this up on your phone, and the settings will carry over to your watch. On your iPhone, go to Settings and tap Siri, then Responses. Select Silent responses instead of Spoken responses. You can then read through her answers, or skim them, as you prefer.

title: Breaking Down the Ending of Jessica Chastain's Nashville Thriller Heartland
content:
Netflix's Heartland follows Misty Jones (Jessica Chastain), a former country music star living in self-imposed exile who returns to Nashville after her niece, an up-and-coming singer named Charlie Heart (Carter Faith), goes missing. As she investigates the disappearance, Misty uncovers a series of suspicious connections involving Charlie's manager, Roy Combs (Garrett Hedlund), and a local police detective. But the biggest revelation is that Charlie's disappearance was all a part of a larger plan to escape someone who had been controlling her for years.

The film's final act explains why Charlie staged her own death, how Misty discovers Roy's involvement, and what happens to the people who enabled him. Here's how the mystery is resolved.

A list of suspects that doesn’t add up

Misty, who walked away from the country music scene nearly 20 years ago after a series of public scandals in Nashville, has little interest in returning to the city. But when her brother Donny asks her to help find his missing daughter, Charlie, she reluctantly agrees. With Donny's wife undergoing cancer treatment, he has no one else to turn to. Charlie, we soon learn, is actually Misty's biological daughter, although she was raised by Donny and his wife.

At first, Misty believes that Charlie may have disappeared voluntarily. Charlie's manager, Roy, tells Misty that the young singer has a history of going off the grid for a few days before returning to her usual routine. The law enforcement officer she turns to for help, Detective White, also seems uninterested in investigating the case in any serious way.

But Misty finds several reasons to question their explanations. While searching Charlie's house, she finds bloodstains in the bedroom, an unfinished song with foreboding lyrics, and a note with a series of numbers. The police suspect that Jared Granger (J.P. Edwards), Charlie's longtime stalker, is responsible for her disappearance. Misty also wonders about Charlie’s boyfriend, fellow country artist Jace Jacobs (Ross Lynch), given the alarmingly high rates of intimate partner violence in general. But when she follows that lead, Jace tells her that their relationship is merely contractual, an act to boost publicity.

The investigation becomes more complicated when Misty breaks into Jared's house, where she finds his collection of photographs and merchandise related to Charlie. Among his possessions there is also a sweatshirt covered in blood, raising suspicion around his connection to the crime.

But Jared maintains that he didn't hurt Charlie. When Jared confronts Misty at his house, he disarms her. Before Misty can get more information from him, Roy arrives and shoots him, thus preventing the stalker from explaining his side of the story or contradicting the evidence. With Jared dead, the police consider the case effectively solved.

For Misty, though, things aren't adding up. At a bar, she sees another customer with a note containing numbers similar to those found at Charlie's house. She recognizes them as betting odds rather than a coded message. She recalls Roy mentioning his gambling addiction. Misty realizes that the evidence against Jared may have been deliberately planted to divert attention from the person actually responsible for Charlie's situation.

When she returns home, she finds Charlie waiting for her.

Why Charlie faked her death

Charlie reveals to Misty that she deliberately disappeared and staged the circumstances of her supposed murder to escape Roy. Although he helped launch her music career, Roy had been exploiting his position of authority over her. He had compromising photographs and videos that he used to blackmail her, threatening to expose the material if she refused to cooperate with him.

Roy's financial problems exacerbated his desperation. He had accumulated substantial gambling debts and taken out a life insurance policy on Charlie. Her death would serve the dual purposes of providing him with much needed money while eliminating someone who could expose his behavior.

Charlie had already tried to get protection from the authorities. She went to the police seeking a restraining order against Roy, but Detective White refused to help her because he was in cahoots with Roy.

With no reliable protection available, Charlie decided to disappear. She created circumstances that suggested she had been murdered and allowed the investigation to point toward Jared, whose obsession with her made him an easy suspect.

After hearing Charlie's account, Misty decides to help her obtain the evidence she needs to expose Roy. She takes her daughter to stay with Winnie Jo Lean (Jennifer Nettles), an old friend who can keep her safe while Misty works on a plan.

What happened between Misty and Winnie Jo Lean

Misty and Winnie have a complicated history in Nashville. Their supposed rivalry became fodder for gossip after an incident in which Misty was accused of punching Winnie in the face. The story contributed to Misty's reputation as difficult and was one of the events that led to her departure from the music scene.

The film eventually reveals that Misty never punched Winnie, but in fact had taken responsibility for a blow dealt by Winnie's abusive ex-husband. Misty accepted the blame because Winnie wasn't ready to go public about the abuse. After Misty brings Charlie to Winnie's home, they arrange a performance at a venue called the Dove, where they eventually sing "Heartland" together.

The performance also serves a practical purpose: Misty needs an opportunity to access Roy's office and retrieve the laptop containing the material he has been using against Charlie. While Misty leaves to carry out her plan, Winnie keeps Roy occupied, performing with him on stage.

Roy meets his fate

Misty manages to enter Roy's office and locate his laptop, which contains the compromising material connected to Charlie and several other victims. But Roy catches on to her and begins to follow her in his truck—the same one he’d used to intimidate Misty earlier in the film, running her off the road.

The confrontation takes place outside Winnie's property. Misty shoots at Roy's approaching vehicle, causing him to lose control and flip the truck. She then cuts off one of his fingers to unlock the laptop and gain access to the evidence.

With the evidence in hand, Charlie can prove Roy's history of blackmail and enable other victims to come forward. Roy is arrested, while Detective White and the police department's involvement in protecting him become subjects of investigation. 

Why Misty goes to prison

Although Misty succeeds in getting the evidence she needs to nail Roy, her violent actions during their confrontation have consequences of their own. She is ultimately arrested and forced to face the consequences of taking matters into her own hands. 

Before turning herself in, Misty visits her former husband, Clark (John Hawkes). Their conversation focuses on Charlie, whom they both continue to share a deep love for despite their complicated past. While Misty is in prison, Charlie visits her and explains that she has released an album independently. She invites her mother to attend one of her performances, but Misty declines. Instead, she tells Charlie that audiences have already heard her sing. Now, it’s her daughter’s turn to have their full attention.

A happy ending for Misty and Charlie

The final scene takes place after Misty has completed her prison sentence. She watches Charlie perform at Nashville's iconic Bluebird Cafe. 

Charlie has moved forward with her music independently, free from the control of anyone with anything but her best interests in mind. Misty, meanwhile, has returned to Nashville, no longer a pariah, ready to support her daughter in a way she never could before the harrowing events they endured together.

title: Inside Salish and Jordan Matter’s Growing Father-Daughter Empire
content:
It’s already 10:27 p.m. on a Saturday night in October when Salish Matter asks gently, “Are we going to start filming soon?”

The 16-year-old stands in the aisle of her local Target in Manhattan Beach, Calif., beside her father Jordan Matter. They are dressed almost identically, in jeans and black shirts. 

The duo is minutes away from filming a video for Jordan’s YouTube channel, which launched in earnest in 2017 and today has more than 38 million subscribers. Over the past several years, Salish has become its star—a role that has helped position her as a pre-eminent teen content creator. With more than 18 million followers across her own TikTok, Instagram, and YouTube accounts, she attracts an audience of teens and tweens who see her as both relatable and aspirational. With Jordan, she is also one half of an increasingly powerful family brand that includes Sincerely Yours, a teen-focused skin-care line that launched last year, and a multiyear talent deal with Netflix, announced in February. The family’s first original series on the streamer, Salish’s 12 Games of Christmas, will premiere Nov. 28, one day before she turns 17.

Tonight’s shoot marks the Matters’ first official collaboration with Target, but the video sits firmly in the family’s milieu: a competition with a frenetic, handheld filming style and bombastic volume. Salish will face off against her father to see who can construct the best sleepover setup using products they find in the store, a riff on Supermarket Sweep. Joining Salish’s team is 34-year-old comedy creator Haley Kalil, a.k.a. Haley Baylee; fellow creators Brooke Monk and Devon Rodriguez will have cameos.

In the aisle, Salish prepares to deliver a line that will kick off nearly five hours of filming, with the creators darting between the shelves as cameras trail them. Jordan encourages his daughter: “Let’s see what you got, Say.” He scans the semicircle of onlookers, largely the family’s team and Kalil’s. The majority are men holding cameras or smartphones. “Everybody, watch how good she is.”

Salish shrugs her shoulders up toward her ears. “No pressure,” Jordan adds.

The morning of the Target shoot, Salish perches on a white bedspread at home. The space around her is sparsely furnished and perfectly neat. There is a white vanity with a mirror, in front of which Salish occasionally films TikToks. On the walls are two posters for the artist SZA, and above the headboard hangs a butter yellow sign with the letters “SY,” a nod to Sincerely Yours. In September 2025, roughly 87,000 people attended its pop-up launch event at the American Dream Mall in New Jersey. Within an hour, the brand sold out at the mall’s Sephora location. Jordan says the crowds were so intense they had to lock the store.

That level of frenzy for a teen content creator—a frenzy that, in past decades, was reserved for pop stars and Hollywood A-listers—is far from out of the ordinary these days. Even a decade ago, young people said they related to content creators more than traditional celebrities-—and many see influencing as the ideal job. A recent study from Edison Research found that 30% of Americans ages 13 to 24 already call themselves digital-content creators.

Though her competition is fiercer than ever, Salish’s rise above the algorithmic fray has a lot to do with her longevity. Despite being only 16, she’s been on kids’ screens for years: “The fact that she’s been doing it consistently, for so long, has allowed these kids to kind of grow up with her,” Jordan says. “Now she’s imprinted in their emotions, as part of their childhood.”

Salish began appearing on her father’s channel in April 2018, at 8 years old. Back then, the channel focused on Jordan’s dance photography—he had already published multiple books—as well as photo challenges with young subjects, including cast members of the reality series Dance Moms and a 14-year-old Tate McRae.

As a kid, Salish loved watching her dad’s videos. When he asked her to join one, she said yes immediately. “I was very shy growing up, and I still am. But I think I came out of my shell a lot,” she says. She speaks melodically and with a slight lisp, grinning. “It was very nerve-racking for me at first to talk in front of a camera, but I got used to it,” she adds. “And now I’m so happy I did it.”

Salish’s appearances on the channel became more frequent during the pandemic, after the family relocated from Nyack, N.Y., to Los Angeles. The family includes her mother Lauren, a trained veterinarian, and her older brother Hudson. Lauren mostly stays off camera. Hudson, now 20, also began appearing on Jordan’s YouTube channel as a child, then pivoted to grow his own.

In 2022, Jordan’s channel hit 10 million subscribers. Two years later, in April 2024, it hit 20 million, and then 30 million in May 2025. So far this year, the channel has garnered more than 3.1 billion views. “It was very obvious that both the audience and I enjoyed the videos where [Salish] was in more,” Jordan says, sitting in the foyer of his home. He is a youthful 60, with an athletic build and strawberry blond hair that stands upright as if he’d touched a live wire. 

As his channel has grown with Salish at its center, Jordan has stepped firmly into the role of strategist. Starting roughly four years ago, he limited their output to once-weekly YouTube videos, eschewing brand deals and product launches until Sincerely Yours. “We wanted to take time to build that emotional connection [with our audience],” Jordan says.

Now, the family’s three-year deal with Netflix is poised to catapult them into a new echelon of recognition. After it was announced, Netflix began hosting select videos from Jordan’s YouTube library. According to the streamer, those videos have spent 14 weeks on the global top 10 chart and entered the top 10 in 75 countries. The new original show, a holiday-themed competition hosted by Jordan, features Salish alongside seven other creators. Together, the group will participate in 12 challenges to win a pile of presents, but there’s a catch: someone among them is an impostor who will try to sabotage the games without the group’s noticing. 

Netflix characterizes the Matters’ deal as unique, even among its recent push to court other content creators and podcasters, including Ms. Rachel and Mark Rober: it includes multiple original titles, rather than one, plus the option to explore additional business deals or partnerships guided exclusively by the streaming giant. “There is no one quite like Salish,” says Heather Tilert, vice president of kids and family series at Netflix. “Her audience’s love for her is undeniable. They connect with her because she’s real and relatable while also being incredibly aspirational and humble.”

Though aspects of Salish’s routine mirror a regular teenager’s—she describes attending a local private high school, doing her homework, and spending time with her friends—she knows there is nothing normal about internet fame. “Since starting content, I’ve just wanted to be normal and have a normal life outside of content,” she says.

Jordan limits filming to Sundays, so Salish can focus on other things the rest of the week. He says he and Lauren are constantly checking in on their daughter’s mental health. “My wife and I talk about it all the time with her,” Jordan says. “Any parent that says, ‘Oh, it’s all good, it’s great—they’re happy.’ Well, maybe they’re happy, but that doesn’t mean it’s all good. There’s still a young person developing into an adult, and now the world is watching them develop.”

Lauren describes her daughter as very private, despite it all: “She is a person with very good boundaries.” Salish doesn’t post about what’s happening in her life behind the scenes—and Lauren says Salish refuses to tell her teachers when she has obligations after hours that might interfere with her performance at school, preferring to keep the two worlds separate. Salish also keeps a low profile with her classmates: “I don’t want to make it my entire personality.”

Jordan says the family is aware of security considerations that arise when sharing children’s lives online, and he points to a note for Salish on the kitchen counter, which was delivered in person and signed by 10 young fans who discovered where they live. To Jordan, the bigger concern is the emotional weight of internet fame: “Seeing where [Salish is] emotionally and how she’s handled it—I don’t see what we could have done better, but that doesn’t mean that everybody should do it,” he says. “We happen to have a kid who seems to be genetically predisposed to be able to handle this kind of life.”

This perspective has not stopped viewers and experts alike from voicing concerns, both about kidfluencing generally and the Matters’ content specifically. In a recent study, professors of entrepreneurship Alisa Jno-Charles of Babson College and Daniel Clark of Western University’s Ivey Business School examine the complexities of kidfluencing as a new form of child labor via an in-depth analysis of four popular family channels. It does not include the Matters, though both Jno-Charles and Clark say their own children watch Salish and Jordan.

“When you are working with your parents, your consent—your understanding of consent—is very different than working with strangers,” says Jno-Charles. “So you theoretically may be asked, ‘Are you OK with this?’ But how comfortable do you feel saying no to your father, whose idea this is?” The stakes can feel particularly high when it comes to a family business: “Continuing this enterprise directly affects his understanding of his career, your family’s net worth, your family’s future. I personally don’t feel like a child is fully capable of removing consent, especially a minor child, in a situation where they’re working with their parent.”

Since the dawn of social media, kidfluencer families like the Matters have shared—and monetized—their children’s lives. Several high-profile cases of alleged exploitation have raised questions about kid creators’ working conditions, access to revenue, and exposure. One prominent recent case involves creator Piper Rockelle, her mother and manager Tiffany Smith, and members of their Los Angeles content collective, known as “the Squad.” In 2022, 11 participants in the collective, all of whom were under 18 at the time, brought a lawsuit against Smith, claiming that she abused them verbally, emotionally, physically, and sexually. (The lawsuit was settled for $1.85 million in 2024; as part of the settlement terms, Smith denied any wrongdoing.) Last year, the case became the subject of the Netflix documentary Bad Influence: The Dark Side of Kidfluencing.

Jordan filmed multiple videos with Rockelle in 2020 and 2021, when she was between 12 and 14, and says he found the documentary shocking. “My experience of it was, it was a relatively healthy environment,” he says. Still, some online commenters have compared the families. Jordan says that he understands the impulse to make a connection, but that those judgments are uninformed. “Almost every opinion comes from people who have never met us,” he says. Lauren adds, “We all realize that people are really imaginative, and a lot of times the comments don’t really have a basis in reality.”

The vast majority of videos on Jordan’s channel feature concepts that are unequivocally child-friendly, like Salish building a secret mall in her home or hiring a fake twin to prank her dad. However, over the years, there have been some that involve crushes or “dates” between Salish and other minors. (Hudson participated in similar videos too.) Salish’s primary “ship”—the pairing her audience is most bought into, which has inspired dozens of fan accounts—is with her best friend, fellow creator Nidal Wonder, 15. In one video, 13-year-old Salish goes on an “emotional first date” with Wonder, 12. In it, Wonder places both hands on Salish’s face, pulling her in as if to kiss her. As their faces inch closer, the camera cuts away. Jordan says Salish and Wonder thought it was funny that people gossiped about whether they were dating back then, and they liked to prank him, pretending to kiss to draw a reaction from him.

Jordan does not see his videos as playing into the idea of a romantic relationship between the pair. “What I’ve always seen with the Nidal thing is I think it’s an incredible opportunity to showcase a very close connection between a boy and a girl that’s not intimate in a romantic way,” Jordan says. 

For her part, Salish says she expects speculation about her personal life but doesn’t let it affect her: “I know that none of the guys I film with, I’m dating, and we’re all just really best friends.”

Jordan says that in his channel’s early years, he relied on his collaborators to tell him what they were comfortable with—and that those suggestions included concepts that might now give him pause. For one shoot, Piper Rockelle, then 13, and another teen re-created well-known romantic celebrity photographs, including a bridal image. “In retrospect, yeah, probably not the best image, especially the wedding-dress part,” he says. 

Like anyone who chooses to showcase their children online, the Matters must contend with the public’s perception of the messages they send. Jordan says he has to think through whether a moment that feels completely normal to him within the context of their private family life could be misconstrued by viewers: “It gets a little frustrating, because there’s so many ways in which people can interpret everything you do.”

The level of scrutiny has become even more intense as the Matters’ profile has risen this year. Recently, for example, some online commentators questioned the propriety of a thumbnail image from Jordan’s YouTube channel that then appeared on Netflix of Salish looking up at the camera with her mouth open. “The fact that we’re getting called out for sexualizing her—it’s completely out of left field because the context of the thumbnail is in no way sexual,” he says. Typically, the family also captures smiling and grimacing versions of thumbnails, but when they A/B test them on the platform, the “shocked” one usually wins out. But Jordan says they’re backing away from using images with the expression to protect Salish nonetheless: “I don’t want Salish to be feeling uncomfortable.” 

At Target, the group finishes shooting around 3 a.m. Salish emerges through the doors of the store into quiet darkness. In the parking lot, members of her crew pack their cars. She takes off toward them in her checkered pajama pants from the shoot. On her feet are gray socks, no shoes. She hugs each person, thanking them. Next week, they’ll move forward, doing it all again.

What does moving forward mean for Salish, in the broader sense? She doesn’t know what her life will look like in five years. She says she knows she wants to continue creating content, and her biggest ambition is to have fun. She’s not sure if she sees herself attending college. Jordan wants his daughter to be able to choose her own adventure. “As she gets older, she has these different buckets that she’s already dipped her toes into, and then she can just pursue them,” he says. “The world is her oyster, honestly.”

Financially, Salish’s future is laid out for her as she ages: according to Jordan, Salish’s share of the family’s gross earnings, which he says is the majority of the profits, is funneled into two trust accounts. Fifteen percent is in a Coogan Blocked Trust Account, which she’ll gain access to when she turns 18. The remaining 85% is in another account, available to her when she’s 25. 

Today, Salish feels fortunate to be in her position, and echoes Jordan’s sentiment about the future: “I feel like I’ve gotten so many amazing opportunities,” she says. “I’ve gotten to see what building a brand is like and what being on a Netflix show is like, and there’s just so many options.” She also lent her voice to the third Angry Birds movie, coming out in December. Recently, while filming TikToks for the movie, Salish was introduced to Kim Kardashian and her son Psalm, who also has a role—the mogul had said they wanted to meet her.

Asked about the hardest part of her job, Salish says there is none: “I’m so lucky that I get to do it. I mean, I don’t even consider it a job.”

title: If Your Google Pixel's Camera Is Suddenly Broken, Here's the Fix
content:
Updates are generally good for your devices. The latest Chrome update, for example, patches an actively exploited security vulnerability, while Apple's latest updates stop people from seeing iMessages they shouldn't have access to. In most cases, it's beneficial to update your tech to the latest software version whenever possible.

Sadly, updates aren't all perfect, as Google Pixel users are discovering this week. As reported by Android Authority, Google's November update apparently shipped with a bug that breaks some Pixel 10 and Pixel 11 cameras. Seeing as Pixels are rather famous for their shooters, this is a decidedly unfortunate glitch.

What's going on with the Pixel's camera?

Here's the situation: Following the November update, some users are opening their Pixel Camera apps to find an error that reads, "Something went wrong. Close and open the Camera app again," with a "Learn More" link to, well, learn more. Others aren't receiving the error, but are instead running into a blank Camera viewfinder, as if the lens is totally covered. What's more, some users are reportedly saying that the issue is present on third-party camera apps, not just the Pixel Camera app. That would imply this is an issue with the camera system-wide, not just the Pixel Camera app itself.

To be clear, it doesn't seem like this is a universal issue. It's not like all Pixel users are now running with broken cameras. But based on the forum complaints Android Authority discovered, it seems reasonable to assume that this glitch isn't limited to just a handful of unlucky Pixel owners.

There's a fix for this Pixel camera bug

Luckily, there is an apparent workaround here, though it's not totally obvious. Some users are having no luck restarting their Pixels, while others report that a factory reset wasn't enough to restore camera functionality.

What does appear to work, however, is shutting your Pixel down and waiting five minutes or so. It's not clear why, but giving your Pixel a chance to "breathe" seems to shake the glitch and bring back your camera. As Android Authority reports, that fix comes from "Diamond and Gold product experts" on Google's Support forum.

If your Pixel's camera is giving you grief following the November update, this workaround is definitely worth a try—especially since more drastic measures don't actually seem to do anything. As the issue does seem to be rather widespread, I wouldn't be surprised to see Google issue a patch in the coming days. But until then, turning your phone off for five minutes may be a decent compromise.

title: 10 Privacy Hacks Every Mac User Should Know
content:
We may earn a commission from links on this page.

Apple has a pretty good track record on privacy. The company bakes a number of protections into its OSes to keep your data from being shared or stolen. That said, you can make your Apple devices even more secure. There are plenty of opt-in settings that make it even harder for anyone to snoop on your device and activity. These are the best privacy hacks for your Mac.

Enable advanced protection for all browsing in Safari to prevent device fingerprinting

Private Browsing in Safari offers some protection against tracking of your device and activity. For example, Safari won't remember searches or save information from form fields, and it will strip link tracking and hide your IP address from known trackers. (Note that Private Browsing does not make you completely anonymous online.) However, these protections don't need to be limited to just Private Browsing. You can also enable advanced tracking and fingerprint protection for regular browsing sessions, which will minimize tracking while keeping other features active. That includes maintaining browsing and search history, allowing autofill, and keeping you logged in to sites that use cookies. You can turn this on by going to Safari > Settings > Advanced and selecting "in all browsing" from the dropdown next to "Use advanced tracking and fingerprint protection."

Turn on Firewall with stealth mode to make your device invisible to network scans

Enabling the macOS Firewall (which is off by default) adds a layer of protection against external devices on your wifi network, as well as unauthorized apps from initiating a connection to your device. Turning on Stealth Mode prevents your Mac from even responding to these requests, essentially making it invisible to anything that's scanning a network you're connected to. This makes it more difficult for hackers and malware to know your device exists, much less attack it. This can interfere with certain essential activity when you're on your home network, but it's a valuable security setting when on public wifi. You can leave Firewall on all the time and enable Stealth Mode only as needed. Go to Settings > Network > Firewall, flip the toggle, then hit Options to manage Stealth Mode.

Enable rotating MAC addresses to prevent activity and location tracking via wifi

Another hack for maintaining privacy on public networks is to enable rotating MAC addresses, which randomizes the identifier your device broadcasts when scanning for and connecting to wifi. If you use either your real MAC address or a fixed one (random but unchanging), it's easier to track your activity on that network, including when you arrive, how long you stay, and when you leave. Rotating addresses are best for public, shared networks you temporarily connect to, and don't require a login via a captive portal (like hotel wifi). You can turn this on for specific networks via Settings > Wi-Fi > [Network Name] > Details and change Private Wi-Fi address to Rotating.

Use "Convert Image Quick Action" to strip metadata from files before sharing

Images and screenshots contain metadata, such as timestamps, device and hardware details, and, in the case of photos, physical location. Much of this information is stripped automatically when you share files to social media or via encrypted messaging apps, but if you're sending them via text or email, posting to forums, or sharing over AirDrop, metadata remains intact. You can easily remove metadata from your images right on your desktop. Select the file and hit control + click to bring up an options menu, then go to Quick Actions > Convert Image. Uncheck the box next to Preserve Metadata, then hit Convert. (This is also useful for quickly converting HEIC to JPEG without opening a separate app.)

Disable diagnostic and analytics sharing to minimize what Apple can use and share with developers

Apple collects information about your device for diagnostic purposes or to improve apps and services, some of which is shared with third-party app developers. This may include crash and usage data as well as recordings and transcripts of Siri interactions and iCloud analytics. You can disable sharing for some or all of these categories under Settings > Privacy & Security > Analytics & Improvements.

Audit and disable location services to prevent background tracking

You may be surprised by the number of apps and system services that use your device's location in the background. You should definitely disable location services for third-party apps that don't require location to function. You can find these toggles under Settings > Privacy & Security > Location Services. You can also turn off location permissions for some Apple apps and services if you're not using them on your device, like Weather and Maps. Finally, tap System Services and disable location for any non-essential features—at the very least, disable "Mac Analytics" and "Significant Locations & routes" (which lets your Mac and other iCloud devices learn locations and routes you use often).

Audit and revoke camera and microphone permissions for inactive apps

Third-party apps on your Mac that need access to your device's camera and microphone have to request permission, and it's easy to grant this in the moment and then forget that you've allowed it. You should regularly audit which apps have these permissions and revoke access from those that don't need them on a day-to-day basis. Disabling them forces the app to ask again. Go to Settings > Privacy & Security > Microphone or Camera to see the allowed apps and flip the toggle to disable permissions.

Restrict local access permissions to prevent utilities or apps from mapping your network

Another permission type you may have granted without much thought is local network access. This allows third-party apps to discover and communicate with other devices—printers, smart speakers, and IoT devices—on your home wifi. While this may be useful for services like Spotify that cast to connected hardware, other utilities, media apps, and games probably don't need to be mapping your network in the background. Go to Settings > Privacy & Security > Local Network to audit permissions and disable those that aren't needed.

Audit and restrict full disk access to keep apps from reading your system

Another important permission to check concerns third-party apps that have access to your Mac's full disk, which includes data from Mail, Messages, Safari, Home, Time Machine, and admin settings. If an app only works with files you explicitly open and save, it doesn't need full disk access. Legitimate use cases may include antivirus and malware scanners, productivity tools, or backup utilities that you trust. You can also audit which apps have access to specific files and folders. This is under Settings > Privacy & Security > Full Disk Access or Files & Folders.

Turn on Advanced Data Protection for iCloud to encrypt your backups end to end

If you're using iCloud to store photos, files, and device backups, your data is encrypted on Apple's servers and in transit. Apple still holds the decryption key, which is useful if you somehow get locked out of your account and need help recovering it, but for sensitive data—including device backups—end-to-end encryption is the most secure way to ensure no one but you can gain access. Advanced Data Protection is an opt-in setting for iCloud that encrypts your information end to end. You'll need to set up an alternative recovery method, such as your device passcode with two-factor authentication, a recovery contact, or a recovery key. Be careful, though: If you lose access to this recovery method, you will lose your data. You can enable Advanced Data Protection on your Mac under System Settings > [Your Name] > iCloud > Advanced Data Protection > Turn On. Note that some iCloud data, including passwords and payment methods, are already end-to-end encrypted by default.

title: These Are the Best Ways to Encrypt Your Email
content:
You probably already know that your email isn't actually all that private, especially if you have a free account with a major service provider like Gmail (Google) or Outlook (Microsoft). But if you are sending sensitive information via email, you can minimize what can be snooped on and by whom using end-to-end encryption, which generally ensures that only the recipient can read your message. Here's what you need to know about email encryption and how to set up an extra layer of privacy.

How email encryption works

As this in-depth explainer from Adaptive Security describes, most emails are encrypted in transit via Transport Layer Security (TLS), which prevents anyone from reading your message as it travels from server to server. However, encryption is temporarily stripped at each server: content is received and processed in plaintext and then re-encrypted when it leaves, meaning it could be read, logged, and distributed by the server provider.

Emails are also typically encrypted at rest—for example, while sitting on Google's servers and in a Gmail recipient's inbox. But this only prevents someone with physical access to the server hardware from reading messages, as Google still holds the encryption key and can access stored data. And, as PCMag points out, Google is scanning your messages to a degree, and it (along with other email providers) can and will hand emails over to law enforcement and government agencies in some cases.

By contrast, with end-to-end encryption (E2EE), emails are readable only on the sender's and recipient's devices, and can be decrypted only with the recipient's private key. They're never translated into plaintext as they pass between and through servers to their destination, meaning that no one—including server providers, hackers, or law enforcement—can view the content. It's worth noting, though, that E2EE is not impenetrable nor a total guarantee of privacy. For example, metadata like subject lines and email addresses may remain in plaintext, and encrypted messages are still susceptible to phishing. Plus, forwarding an encrypted message breaks the encryption.

Still, end-to-end encryption is especially useful when sending sensitive information that may be valuable to bad actors, though if security and privacy are a high priority, you may want to consider it for all of your emails. How you deploy encryption depends on whether you are adding it to your current email or switching to a dedicated provider.

Add third-party encryption to your existing email

If you have an account with a major email provider like Gmail, Outlook, or Apple Mail, you can add a third-party tool that layers an encryption protocol like OpenPGP on top of your existing account. PCMag recommends PreVeil, SecureMyEmail, and Virtru (which is limited to Gmail users in Chrome) for those who want to keep their current emails. Mailvelope is a browser add-on (and therefore a desktop-only tool) available in Chrome, Firefox, and Edge, though it can also be installed on other browsers, like Brave, that are built on the same architecture. FlowCrypt integrates with Gmail and Google Workspace on desktop and mobile.

Note that enterprise users of Google Workspace and Microsoft 365 have access to true end-to-end encryption without third-party add-ons. Gmail's Confidential mode and Outlook's Encrypt feature, available to all users, are not E2EE equivalents, as Google and Microsoft, respectively, still manage the keys.

Switch to a dedicated encrypted email provider

For those who are willing to start fresh with a new email address (or who have a custom domain), providers like Proton Mail or Tuta offer native end-to-end encryption. The caveat: by default, this is only between users on the same service, so from one Proton user to another. If you want to send an end-to-end encrypted email from Proton to a Gmail user, for example, you have to set up password protection (and share the password via another secure channel) or use a PGP-compatible tool like those listed above. You can also Proton's Gmail integration does allow for end-to-end encryption, but only if both Gmail parties are using the Proton integration.

The bottom line here is that email wasn't designed to be a highly secure form of communication. End-to-end encryption does add a layer of privacy and security if you jump through hoops to set it up, but it's still susceptible to human error and social engineering.

Black Friday FAQs

When is the best time of the year to save the most? 

Prime Day and Black Friday are the two best times of the year to get the best deals on most purchases. Of course, depending on what you're shopping for, you might find other opportunities throughout the year, but in general, Prime Day and Black Friday have the best sales.

Are Cyber Monday deals better than Black Friday?

Black Friday used to be bigger for major retailers and more expensive tech and appliances, while Cyber Monday was better for cheaper tech and gave smaller businesses a chance to compete online. Nowadays, though, the distinction is almost meaningless. Every major retailer will offer sales on both days, and the smart move is to know what you want, do your research, or refer to guides like our Black Friday and Cyber Monday coverage that have done all the vetting for you.

How do I make the most of Black Friday? 

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

title: 10 Books Like ‘A Court of Thorns and Roses’ You Should Read Next
content:
We may earn a commission from links on this page.

Sarah J. Maas’ lush, romance-soaked series A Court of Thorns and Roses has blossomed into a sprawling, complex fantasy series with millions of dedicated fans, and with good reason. A complex heroine who keeps discovering new depths in herself, fascinating supporting characters who shift from antihero to antivillain in unexpected ways, creative and beautifully rendered world-building—the series has it all, while also being unapologetically romantic (and steamy).

The story of a huntress who is kidnapped by a fae prince and brought to the Spring Court as a prisoner, only to become a key player in all that fae drama, ACOTAR is special, but Maas can only write so fast. If you need more books with the same lush feel, here are 10 to get you started.

House of Flame and Shadow, by Sarah J. Maas (2024)

It’s no shock that one of Sarah J. Maas’ other series would be recommended for fans of A Court of Thorns and Roses, but there’s a specific reason you should jump into her Crescent City series, especially the third book, House of Flame and Shadow. The most recent ACOTAR book, A Court of Splintered Harmony, revealed that the events of House of Flame and Shadow tie directly into the events in Splintered Harmony, particularly with regard to the character of Feyre’s sister, Nesta. In other words, if you read Splintered Harmony and wondered why Nesta was being so weird, there’s a whole other book series you should dig into immediately.

title: Microsoft Officially Apologized for Yesterday's Outages
content:
If you were having trouble accessing certain services like Microsoft Teams or Outlook, you were not alone. Early Thursday afternoon, many of Microsoft's biggest apps and services were experiencing downtime. According to Downdetector, which tracks user reports of issues with websites and platforms, Microsoft 365, Teams, Copilot, Teams, and OneDrive were all experiencing issues. As of Friday afternoon, Microsoft has restored service to many users, and has officially apologized for the outages.

Which Microsoft services were affected by the outages?

When I first published this article on Thursday, I couldn't even load Microsoft 365's status page. (I've reported on many service outages, but I can't recall a time when a service's status page was also down.) Even as of Friday afternoon, the page still says "Service degradation on Microsoft 365 (Business or Enterprise)," and Microsoft says the following services may be affected: Exchange Online, Microsoft 365 admin center, Microsoft 365 apps, Microsoft 365 Apps Admin Center, Microsoft 365 Education, Microsoft Copilot 365, Microsoft Defender for Office 365, Microsoft Defender XDR, Microsoft Fabric, Microsoft Graph, Microsoft Intune, Microsoft Planner, Microsoft Power Apps, Microsoft Purview, Microsoft Teams, Microsoft To Do, Power BI, SharePoint Online, Universal Print, and Windows 365.

Looking specifically at Outlook, Microsoft's email service had hundreds of thousands of user reports Thursday afternoon, signaling a major issue somewhere in Microsoft's pipeline. The reports did "slow down" throughout the day, but Downdetector still showed over 50,000 reports coming in every 15 minutes when I checked Thursday afternoon.

What caused these Microsoft outages?

While the root cause of the issue was a mystery throughout Thursday's outage, Microsoft confirmed the problem in an apology on Friday. According to the company, "This was a technical issue not related to cyber or AI [or] agents. The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change. We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions."

Microsoft says it is "deeply sorry" for the disruption to its customers and partners. The company says the fix rolled out slower than some might expect, since it wanted to restore service gradually to evaluate stability at each stage. It also says it will release a full post-incident report once it completes a review.

During the outage, the company had confirmed that some of its infrastructure was experiencing elevated load, which it said was likely contributing to the issues. Microsoft then said it was pausing all deployments and moving traffic from affected infrastructure, and that it found that a number of its servers were unexpectedly unavailable after failing health checks. The company then thought a specific component responsible for processing server health may be the reason the system is failing health checks. Microsoft said an alternative service health check method successfully restarted some of the affected servers. The company was then actively restarting and validating affected servers to bring them back to service.

title: How Texas’ Blue Takeover Could Soon Begin Impacting Texans’ Lives
content:
Texas has long been led by Republicans, from its governor’s mansion and state legislature down to many of its locally held offices. But this year’s elections have abruptly turned the ruby-red state blue, with sweeping implications for Texas’ laws and the lives of its more than 30 million residents. 

Democrats scored a series of historic victories in Texas state politics earlier this month, winning every statewide race on the ballot and a number of more local contests to boot. Gina Hinojosa upset Gov. Greg Abbott to become the state’s first-ever Latina governor and the first Democrat elected to the position since the 1990s. Democratic candidates swept up key posts in the races for lieutenant governor, attorney general, comptroller, and land and agricultural commissioners. In the state House, Democrats won a majority for the first time in over two decades. 

On a statewide level, only the Texas Senate, the state’s Supreme Court and court of criminal appeals, and the railroad commission remain under Republican control. And while they didn’t win the majority in the latter three bodies, Democrats gained significant ground there, too. For the first time since 1990, the party claimed one of the state’s three railroad commissioner positions.In the races for Texas’ state courts, meanwhile, Democratic candidates managed to secure three of nine seats on the criminal appeals court and four of nine on the state Supreme Court, smashing another decades-long streak of Republican victories several times over. The last time any Democrat had been elected to either court was in 1994.

Read More: What Just Happened in Texas Changes Everything

Experts tell TIME that these victories could impact Texans across the state in a variety of areas—and soon. 

In January, newly elected officials in Texas’ executive branch will begin their terms. The new slate of Texas lawmakers will also convene that month for their first legislative session, in which they will propose and vote on legislation.

Here are some of the most significant—and quickest—ways in which the state’s blue takeover could affect Texans’ lives.

Immigration

One area in which newly elected Texas Democrats have indicated they will change course: combatting President Donald Trump’s aggressive immigration crackdown.

During her gubernatorial campaign, Hinojosa accused Abbott of facilitating “fatal ICE operations” in the state and called on the governor to “lead with responsibility and decency by refusing to provide state resources until DHS stops killing U.S. citizens and detaining our children.”

Shortly after Trump returned to the White House last year, Abbott issued multiple Executive Orders directing state agencies to coordinate and assist with the Trump Administration’s immigration operations. The Republican governor also previously signed into law a controversial measure, SB 4, that requires cities and counties to share information regarding the immigration status of detained individuals with federal officers.

Read More: As ICE Detention Expands, Deaths Reach a 22-Year High

Abbott has pursued a hard-line immigration agenda of his own in recent years as well, transporting migrants from Texas to Democratic-led cities and launching an initiative aimed at combatting illegal immigration in the state, Operation Lone Star, that has seen thousands of Texas National Guard and Department of Public Safety (DPS) officers deployed to the southern border and the state work to erect a number of physical barriers there.

Attorney General-elect Nathan Johnson has said that he would review state agreements with Immigration and Customs enforcement (ICE), allowing him to have “private individual investigative authority over actions by ICE committed in my state.” And following the elections earlier this month, Houston Mayor John Whitmire has already instructed city police to limit cooperation with ICE officers through an Executive Order. 

Josiah Heyman, a professor of border studies at the University of Texas El Paso, notes that SB 4 “is still in place,” but says that “certainly a great deal matters in terms of how it's carried out, how it's interpreted.” 

“What they could change would be the ways that the Texas law enforcement cooperates with the ICE and Customs and Border Protection. I think that's far and away the most important thing that could be done,” Heyman tells TIME.

He says that Democratic leaders may increasingly push back against SB 4 by directing reduced cooperation with ICE, and eventually attempt to repeal the law entirely. “There's an enormous amount of discretion that could be exercised in assigning officers,” he says. He cautions, however, that “it's going to take a while for changes to take place in the actual laws themselves.” 

Faisal Al Juburi, the co-CEO of RAICES, a non-profit legal aid organization serving the Texas immigrant community, tells TIME that there could also be an end to family detention in Texas following the change in the state’s leadership, noting that this is “one of the key areas that has appeared to be a focus” for Hinojosa. The governor-elect has vowed to stop private prison companies from holding children and their families in immigration detention in the state. 

Al Juburi says that the South Texas Family Residential Center in Dilley, Texas, currently the sole migrant family detention facility in the U.S., could potentially be shuttered shortly after Democratic officials take office. 

‘That is an area where there's the potential for some action to happen right out of the gate,” he says.

Data centers 

Several newly elected officials have also promised to restrict the rapid growth of data centers, which have been a source of discontent for many Texans, who have expressed concerns over the centers draining water supplies, driving up energy costs, and creating unwanted noise and pollution. 

Hinojosa said last month that she would issue a moratorium on all data center approvals and proposed requirements for companies to show that their facilities would not drive up water and electricity costs for residents living nearby. Lieutenant governor-elect Vikki Goodwin has also vowed to “prioritize bills that regulate data centers and protect our water, land, health, and access to electricity,” while Agriculture Commissioner-elect Clayton Tucker said that he would issue impact studies on data centers’ effect on Texas water and farmlands. “I stand with the Texas Farmers Union, the people of Hill County, and all of the Texans who are calling to stop data centers,” Tucker said. 

Read More: How AI Backlash Shaped the 2026 Midterms

Kenneth Medlock, a senior director at Rice University’s Center for Energy Studies, tells TIME that data centers are going to be at the “top of the ledger” when it comes to creating new energy-related policy. 

He notes, however, that Hinojosa’s promised moratorium could only apply to new projects, and that there isn’t much she could do about those that are ongoing. 

“Anything, even on the data center front, that's already under construction, is not going to get suspended or disrupted,” he says. “This is really going to be more about how things change going forward.”

Due to data centers’ contributions to the state’s economy, though, Medlock also doesn’t see a version of Texas in which data centers cease to exist entirely. 

“You're going to see some interesting developments in the interest of preserving business expansion while also minimizing community and environmental impact,” he says. 

Education

Texas’ private and public school systems could also see sweeping changes impacting millions of students under the state’s new leadership. 

One of the earliest changes on that front could come as soon as Hinojosa’s first day in office, when she has pledged to fire Texas Education Agency (TEA) Commissioner Mike Morath. 

“Installing a new commissioner of education is a clear authority within the new governor's office, that will have huge implications for our education policy as it stands and how things might might look going forward,” Chloe Sikes, who leads policy research across Texas for the Intercultural Development Research Association (IDRA), tells TIME. She says that this position will be crucial in enforcing potential education reform if new laws are enacted. 

A potential target for such reform is Texas’ Bluebonnet Learning curriculum, a state-owned curriculum developed under Abbott’s Administration that has drawn controversy for its inclusion of Bible-related teachings and materials that critics contend downplay the role of racism and slavery in U.S. history.

“That could be clearly rolled back depending on the leadership the governor-elect wants to develop at the state board level,” Sikes says of the curriculum.

David DeMatthews, a professor of Education at the University of Texas, Austin, adds that Hinojosa may also roll back Texas’ A-F accountability system, which assigns public schools and districts letter grades based on student achievement. The program has faced backlash over its disproportionate impact in districts serving low-income students and the harsh penalties that can be levied against schools that receive poor grades, including state takeovers in which local school boards are replaced by state-appointed managers. 

“I would expect that local control would be returned to those school districts relatively quickly,” DeMathews tells TIME. “What that means for parents is they can kind of show back up to a school board meeting with people they voted for and impress upon them their concerns or their desires.”

DeMatthews also says that Texas’ state voucher program, which enables parents to put taxpayer money toward students’ private school educations, could also end in the near future. Critics of the program have argued that its funds should be used for the state’s public school system.

The voucher program, DeMatthews explains, was established as part of a state law, which would need to be repealed by passing both chambers of the state House. But Hinojosa has veto power to reject future appropriations for the program.

“There will be no voucher money to be appropriate to families … That may leave some families in a position where they're going to no longer attend the private school,” he says. He notes, however, that “the overwhelming majority of families that are using the voucher already have their kids in private schools.”

Reproductive healthcare 

Texas bans abortion in almost all cases, with narrow exceptions in cases when the life or health of the pregnant person is deemed to be at risk.

Under the state’s current Attorney General, Republican Ken Paxton, Texas has sued multiple out-of-state doctors for allegedly violating its laws restricting abortion by mailing abortion pills into the state. But Texas’ incoming top prosecutor, Johnson, has stated that he would not do the same. 

“The first thing I do when people ask me about abortion is point out that I’m not a legislator, and I can’t change abortion law.” Johnson told The Texas Tribune after the elections earlier this month. “What I can do is cease using Texas abortion laws as an instrument of persecution and intimidation, harassment and political showboating. All four of those things have happened.”

Hinojosa has also voiced support for abortion rights and vowed to “prioritize making sure that doctors are no longer prosecuted” in the state for providing abortions in medical emergencies.

Read More: 'An Exodus of OB-GYNs': How the Dobbs Decision Has Shaken the Reproductive Health Landscape

“As governor, I will ensure that every woman has the right to privacy, dignity, and care,” Hinojosa said in January. “Traveling the state, I’ve heard countless stories from women who are afraid to get pregnant, and I want to remind them that they are not alone.”

Raven Freeborn, executive director of Avow, a Texas-based abortion access advocacy organization, tells TIME that declining to continue Paxton’s enforcement techniques would open the door for expanding access to reproductive healthcare across Texas. 

“We're talking about increasing investment in programs that support pregnant and parenting Texans,” Freeborn says. “We can see the shrinking of reproductive healthcare deserts. We can see the return of quality providers across the state.”

LGBTQ+ rights

Ash Hall, a policy and advocacy strategist at the American Civil Liberties Union of Texas, tells TIME that the blue wave in Texas could also result in the state easing restrictions targeting the LGBTQ+ community. 

“We do think that the governor, the attorney general, state agencies, they're all going to have a role to play in stopping the harm and the terrorization that trans Texans have gone through from the government,” Hall says. 

One change they predict the newly elected officials could make is overturning a state law that requires patients’ biological sex to be used on their medical records.

“Instead of everybody being forced to go by their name assigned at birth or their gender assigned at birth, for example, we're hoping doctors will have more leeway to treat trans and intersex patients with dignity and respect,” Hall says. 

Johnson has said, for instance, that he will not devote resources to enforcing a Texas law restricting transgender people’s access to bathrooms. 

Read More: As Texas Targets Trans Youth, a Family Leaves in Search of a Better Future

Though same-sex marriage is legal in all states, Hall adds that Texas’ Constitution includes language saying the practice is banned, while an “anti-sodomy” provision also still exists within the state’s Penal Code. Hall contends these texts, which are unenforceable due to landmark Supreme Court rulings, could soon be removed. 

Following the elections, some transgender Texans who were previously planning to leave the state have reportedly reconsidered.  

“It's nice that things aren't going to get worse, and we can finally focus on how to make things better,” Hall says. “It's a new era for us.”

title: What An Early Polar Vortex Combined With El Niño Means For Winter Weather
content:
A record-early breakdown of the polar vortex is expected to bring cold weather to the United States by the end of the month.

The expected wobble in the polar vortex that sends Arctic temperatures south, however, could be in competition with the strong El Niño forecast for this winter—but experts say that how it will impact our weather remains to be seen. 

What is the polar vortex?

The polar vortex is a low-pressure band of air centered over the North Pole in the stratosphere, where it typically sits close to the pole and rotates cyclonically around the region. 

Every few winters, the polar vortex will be disrupted, causing what is known as sudden stratospheric warming, in which temperatures in the stratosphere jump by 50-70 degrees in a few days. That can displace cold air, pushing it down towards parts of North America, Europe, or Asia.

A wobbly polar vortex can shape weather in the northern hemisphere—though it typically takes a few weeks for its impact to be felt. The breakdown causes cold air that is usually trapped to spill out of the Arctic toward lower latitudes, triggering a cold snap. “If the polar vortex gets disrupted and weakens, then that cold air tends tends to be released southward into the mid-latitudes, and of course, with more cold air, you can also have an increased chance or risk of snowstorms or ice storms,” says Judah Cohen, a climate scientist at MIT.

The polar vortex disruption currently being observed by meteorologists is the earliest ever recorded, as it typically weakens during the second half of winter. “Typically we think of this happening toward the end of the winter, in January or February,” says Andrew Charlton-Perez, professor of meteorology at the University of Reading. “So what's unusual about this event is that it's the earliest recorded sudden warming event.” 

How will the polar vortex interact with El Niño? 

The polar vortex is expected to bring chilly temperatures to the U.S. by Thanksgiving week. However, what happens beyond that is still uncertain. 

A weak polar vortex in November by no means dictates the rest of the winter. “This is not going to determine how our winter is going to be,” says Cohen. “It could make it colder right at the start of winter, but I don't think its influence will last much longer than that.”

Experts say that it’s too early to say how the so-called “super El Niño” might interact with the polar vortex. “Because these events are so rare, we have perhaps 45 or so of these events that we've ever observed,” says Charlton-Perez. 

El Niño years typically bring milder temperatures, but much depends on how it interacts with the polar vortex over the rest of the winter. 

There’s a chance El Niño and the polar vortex work together, which would mean this winter would have mild weather in store. “If the pole vortex is in a strong circular state [for the rest of winter], then it's going to influence our weather to be mild, and the El Niño influences our weather to be mild, so they're reinforcing each other,” says Cohen. 

However, if the El Niño and polar vortex work against each other, what the weather looks like could just depend on which force wins out. 

“If the polar vortex weakens and wobbles and meanders around the northern hemisphere, then the polar vortex is really favoring [colder weather] so then it'll be a battle,” Cohen adds.

Just how it all plays out remains to be seen. 

“We've never had a polar vortex disruption of this magnitude and a super El Nino,” says Cohen. “So in some ways, this is uncharted territory.”

title: Microsoft Struggles to Repair Worldwide Outage. Here's What You Need to Know
content:
An outage affecting Microsoft services including Outlook, Teams, and Copilot has stretched into a second day, leaving businesses and governments around the world struggling to access email communications.

As of Friday midday ET, almost 24 hours since the outage was first reported, Microsoft said it was observing "signs of sustained recovery" across its services, with email queues "approaching normal levels." Full recovery efforts continued.

The company reported "no evidence of malicious activity associated with the incident" at this time.

"This was a technical issue not related to cyber or AI/agents. The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change. We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions," Microsoft said in an update.

Outlook and Teams are widely-used workplace applications, with hundreds of millions of users. The disruption to the services left some affected workers unable to access their emails, host meetings, or complete other Microsoft-dependent office tasks.

Governments and companies impacted worldwide

The U.S. House of Representatives was impacted by the Microsoft outage, its communications department told TIME. The House's technology teams worked with Microsoft to restore email access for its members "as quickly as possible."

Municipal governments across the United States were still encountering significant system issues Friday morning, with digital communications interrupted.

Baltimore County Government said its staff were "unable to send or receive emails due to the widespread Microsoft outage,” but assured the public that 911 and other essential county services had not been affected. Offices belonging to the City of Jacksonville, Florida, and City of Austin, Texas, reported similar disruptions to email capabilities. 

Tech businesses also faced disruptions to their day-to-day operations.

Users of two leading artificial intelligence companies, OpenAI and Anthropic, reported failures involving Microsoft 365 integration tools.

Overseas, the U.K. government said it was still “experiencing problems sending and receiving emails.”

The outage also impacted Britain’s National Health Service (NHS), raising concerns about access to appointments and hospital schedules. Some NHS practices reported not being able to send or receive emails. Patients were advised to make contact via phone rather than using email. As a result, some NHS boards warned of an increased demand across phone lines.

In Japan, lawmaker Masanao Ozaki said the outage had affected the government's IT infrastructure and that officials were “closely watching the company's response.” Elsewhere, the Philippines' Supreme Court warned that “responses to emails and other transactions may be delayed.”

In India, the outage disrupted operations at several airlines, with IndiGo and Akasa Air reporting problems related to its customer-support email services.

In Australia, federal bodies including intelligence agency ASIO and the Australian Federal Police were affected. Home Affairs and Cyber Security Minister Tony Burke reiterated that Microsoft did not believe it was dealing with a cyberattack, suggesting the disruption could instead be related to a faulty software update.

"They believe they are dealing in some ways similar ‌to what we saw with respect to CrowdStrike, where there is an update that has gone awry," Burke said during a press conference.

A major Microsoft IT outage in 2024 grounded flights, sent TV stations off air, and disrupted online hospital systems. The malfunction was linked to a third party, a cybersecurity technology firm named CrowdStrike. 

How Microsoft is responding 

Microsoft acknowledged initial reports of an outage Thursday afternoon, just before 1 p.m. ET, with outage-tracking website Downdetector.com recording nearly 130,000 reports of Outlook problems.

In the hours that followed, Microsoft continued to issue updates as its engineers worked to restore affected services. The company said it would restart and repair impacted infrastructure, before gradually bringing the services back online.

Engineers were also exploring additional measures, such as actively restarting and validating affected servers and using automated recovery systems to find and restart unresponsive servers, in an effort to speed up the process.

TIME has reached out to Microsoft for further information.

This isn’t the first time Microsoft has experienced an outage. In addition to the 2024 CrowdStrike incident, the company also experienced disruptions affecting Microsoft 365 in January this year and flagged connectivity issues across multiple regions with its Azure cloud platform in October last year.

A return to faxes and phones

The Microsoft outage has prompted some offices to resort to older forms of technology.

Traders in Japan have reported a return to analog measures, sending faxes to get deals over the line rather than using email confirmations.
Ryutaro Kimura, a Tokyo-based senior bond strategist at BNP Paribas Asset Management, told Bloomberg that trading itself is largely unaffected as "desks were still getting trades done by phone and fax."

Companies across the country's leading industries have also urged customers to avoid email in the interim. Tokyo International Air Cargo Terminal, for example, told customers to reach out via phone or fax.
