title: How Movies About Tech Turned Dystopian
content:
In 2014, a film about a prickly, arrogant inventor trying to build a “machine that can solve any problem” arrived in theaters. It explored the secretive creation of a powerful technology that enabled a group of military leaders to unilaterally determine the life and death of thousands.

From the vantage point of 2026, the story sounds unsettling, even dystopian. But The Imitation Game was actually a celebration of its protagonist, Alan Turing, and his pivotal role in helping the Allies decrypt German intelligence messages en route to victory in World War II. The movie was a box-office smash, won an Oscar, and exemplified a slew of Obama-era, techno-optimist movies that celebrated rugged individuals relentlessly building futuristic tech that could lead to a better society. 

How times have changed. This fall, a new crop of movies arrives that essentially serves as a rejection of that thesis and a damning referendum on the past decade in tech. In the eyes of these movies, tech titans have used their power to exacerbate violent extremism (Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning); undermine democratic norms (Elon Musk in Musk); mislead the public (Elizabeth Holmes in You Can See Everything); and play roulette with the future of humanity (Sam Altman in Artificial). 

In some cases, the films seem to spill from depiction into outright activism. In The Social Reckoning, for example, the protagonists trying to hold Zuckerberg accountable contend that the only way to get powerful people to change is to “cause pain.” And pain Hollywood can certainly cause: tech companies have invested hundreds of billions of dollars to make AI a pillar of society, and face a financial bloodbath should the public reject their tools. 

But the damning tone of these films could also prove to be self-sabotaging, because Hollywood is mostly controlled by a handful of billionaires who are heavily invested in AI—and building AI tools that can replace artists. And they have already begun striking back. Musk threatened to sue Musk director Alex Gibney for defamation, and in June, Amazon’s movie arm abruptly dropped Artificial from its slate; the company has a $50 billion investment in Altman’s OpenAI. (Neon subsequently picked up the film.) Time will tell whether these films land their intended blow against Big Tech—or represent the last-ditch resistance of a creative class indebted to overlords they abhor.

Tech and Hollywood Mythmaking

These films are remarkably different in their storytelling approach. Gibney’s documentary Musk is a methodical four-hour march through the Tesla founder’s corporate foibles; Aaron Sorkin’s drama The Social Reckoning traces the growing personal disillusionment of eventual Facebook whistleblower Frances Haugen (Mikey Madison). You Can See Everything unfolds as something of a psychological chess match between Theranos’ Elizabeth Holmes, who is trying to rehabilitate her image right before she heads to prison, and filmmakers Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, who hope to interrogate her contradictions. 

But they all converge on one central question: Why are these flawed titans the way they are? In 1941, Orson Welles’ Citizen Kane set the template for generations of Hollywood character portraits—that the burning ambition of an antihero can be often traced back to searing moments of emotional pain. Both The Imitation Game and The Social Network, two prominent 2010s tech movies, follow this tradition by giving Turing and Zuckerberg their own Rosebuds in the form of past heartbreak. These framings rationalize their later harmful actions, as if to say that tech geniuses get hurt and then lash out just like the rest of us. 

This new crop of films, however, largely comes to the opposite conclusion: that these tech overlords have charted a wayward course for humanity precisely because of how differently—and callously—they think. In the aughts, Peter Thiel and other members of the so-called PayPal Mafia came to the conclusion that the path to Silicon Valley success required chasing relentless speed and scale at any cost. This new playbook dictated that founders bet everything on a company vision; sell the public on the myth, even if parts were untrue; scheme and scrap toward invention and then monopoly; then rinse and repeat on an even bigger scale. 

This approach has created some of the world’s biggest companies. But the movies argue it also baked failure, deception, and collateral damage into the process. And instead of trying to solve for heroic missions—like beating back the Nazis—these new tech heroes’ main goal seemed to be acquiring, addicting, and monetizing as many users as possible. 

These new movies grapple with this psychological shift. As the screenwriter of The Social Network in 2010, Aaron Sorkin painted Zuckerberg as petulant, to be sure, but still soulful, and hellbent on sticking it to the man. A quarter-century later, the Zuckerberg he wrote and directed Jeremy Strong to play in Reckoning is the man: robotic and cruel, making decisions via cold cost analysis. In Luca Guadagnino’s Artificial, Andrew Garfield plays Sam Altman as a serial liar who will say anything if it helps further his mission. These guys aren’t depicted as antiheroes, but as villains, with self-serving worldviews that may be incompatible with democracy. 

AI Anxiety

Their worldviews pose even more dangers as they shift their focus from social media to AI. The film that most directly deals with current AI harms is not part of this mainstream Hollywood crop but the documentary NAZA, shot in Tel Aviv by two Oscar-winning Israeli directors. Under cover of darkness, anonymous Israeli officers describe how AI tools enabled mass surveillance and bombing in Gaza. The tools allowed them to think about war as a video game, and their victims not as people but as “ants” or a “factory of targets.” (The IDF has rejected many of the movie’s claims.)

Musk and Artificial carry even more apocalyptic overtones. The former ends with a visualization of Musk flying off into space on a rocket ship as the earth explodes behind him. Gibney told TIME in September that his dread levels these days are “really high.” “Elon Musk is betting on whether or not AI will lead us to a moment of extraordinary abundance or basically the end of life on earth,” he said. “Who makes that kind of a bet?” 

Read More: Elon Musk Calls This Documentary a 'Hit Piece.' Here’s Why It’s So Critical of Him

This Time, It's Personal

What will the overwhelming negativity of these movies achieve? Gibney hopes to offer a holistic and rigorous examination of the character of tech leaders, who are constantly pivoting out of crises and toward the Next Big Thing. Musk has moved from cars to rockets to the government to AI and back. Zuckerberg changed Facebook’s name to Meta amid the backlash brought on by Haugen’s whistleblowing—and then when the metaverse fell flat, he dumped all of his company’s money into AI. 

Film offers viewers a more deeply engaging escape from the algorithmic hamster wheel and undeniably shapes public perception. Elizabeth Holmes says so herself in You Can See Everything, at least according to filmmaker Fielder: that many people who met Holmes in prison believed that The Dropout, a fictionalized Hulu series starring Amanda Seyfried, was a documentary about her. 

That hostility coursing through these movies matters, because AI ambitions depend on mass adoption. To train ever more powerful AI, companies like OpenAI and Meta have borrowed hundreds of billions of dollars, which they will eventually need to repay by earning consistent and massive revenue. The public is already immensely distrustful of AI, even as they adopt it in huge numbers. If Artificial persuades many people to stop using ChatGPT—as Andrew Garfield has done—that could put further pressure on the industry’s wager.

But much of these would-be viewers already dislike Big Tech—while many others are simply disengaged, preferring to do literally anything else with their free time than obsess over tech leaders. The Social Reckoning has made just $17 million, a far cry from The Social Network’s $225 million rake, and Musk has grossed $730,000 despite strong reviews. (You Can See Everything has fared better, but that may be more because of the fascination surrounding Fielder than Holmes.) 

The tech titans themselves seem to care, though, and are responding in kind. They are increasingly withholding access from journalists or TV interviews, opting instead for friendlier settings like The Joe Rogan Experience. They are shaping how these films are perceived on social media: multiple platforms initially declined to run Musk’s trailer because of its “political content.” They own the film studios, and could cut off funding for similarly critical products, relegating them to the less widely seen indie margins. And finally, they are building AI tools which could make many of the human elements of the filmmaking process obsolete—virtual actors, animation, set design, storyboarding. 

Given all of these threats, perhaps it’s not a surprise that these tech movies thrum with urgency and apocalyptic rhetoric. As the famous tagline for Jaws: The Revenge read, “This time, it’s personal.” So Hollywood is snapping back, casting itself as an embattled underdog in a fight for its life. The problem is that it’s already sitting inside Big Tech’s gaping mouth.

title: Breaking Down the Hard-Won Ending of The Good Daughter
content:
Warning: This post contains spoilers for The Good Daughter finale.

Charlie Quinn (Meghann Fahy) is out the farmhouse door before the man on the lawn can reach the porch, her hair flying behind her, her voice barely above a whisper. What is he doing here, she wants to know. Mason “Huck” Huckabee (Jake McDorman) asks whether her sister is home. Her husband is, Charlie warns him. Huck says he is sorry about her father’s death. Behind the screen door, Samantha Quinn (Rose Byrne) has come close enough to hear him add that he has to speak with them both, and it’s important. Huck has been to this house before. The first time, he wore a mask, though Charlie doesn’t yet know that it was him behind that mask.

This confrontation opens the finale of The Good Daughter, Peacock’s six-part limited series adapted by Karin Slaughter, who wrote every episode, from her 2017 novel. More than 20 years earlier, two masked men came into the Quinn kitchen in Pikeville, Georgia, looking for Rusty (Brendan Gleeson), a defense attorney who represented the people nobody else in town would. They found his wife, Gamma (Olivia Williams), and his daughters instead. They killed Gamma. Sam took a bullet to the head and was left for dead. Charlie, the younger sister, escaped after Zach Culpepper sexually assaulted her. Police arrested Zach, who went to prison, and they shot dead his brother, Daniel, whom they named as the second assailant. The Culpepper family has always insisted Daniel was innocent, and we learn in the finale that they were telling the truth.

In the years that followed, the sisters grew up and then apart, Sam to patent law in New York, Charlie to a public defender’s desk in the town where it happened, until a fight in New York left them estranged. What draws them back together is a shooting at the local school that kills the principal, Doug Pinkman, and a young student named Emma. Kelly Wilson (Shayna Benardo), an intellectually disabled teenager who tends to tell people what they want to hear, is found with the gun in her hand, and Rusty takes her case. Huck teaches at the school, and Charlie had recently spent a night with him. Rusty dies quietly one night in Episode 4, before he can see the case through. By the finale, Sam has taken up Kelly’s defense, and Charlie has at last told her sister what Zach did to her in the woods.

The finale, “What Really Happened,” solves both crimes within its first 40 minutes, and the culprits are the same as in Slaughter’s novel. The aftermath is where the series largely goes its own way, changing a prison sentence and letting the sisters find a vital piece of their past together. “I’ve written a lot of crime novels, and one thing I think is very important to readers and viewers as well is this: a feeling that justice has been done, and that there’s hope, and those are very important guiding lights to all my writing,” Slaughter tells TIME. In this finale, whatever justice and hope the sisters find comes only after they have told each other the truth.

The second masked man

Within minutes of the episode’s opening, Sam accuses Huck of an older crime: burning down the Quinns’ house more than 20 years ago, shortly before the masked men came. Back then, Huck’s sister, Annalie, had testified that a man raped her. Rusty was the man’s lawyer and, by Huck’s account, tore her apart on the stand. That same week, the family’s house went up in flames. “It was him,” Sam says. “He threw the Molotov cocktail.” Huck turns back with wet eyes. He says the fire was meant as a warning, but Rusty was back in court the next day. Annalie later died by suicide, and Huck, then 17, found her body. He blames Rusty for her death.

Ben (Michael Dorman), Charlie’s estranged husband, who has worked as a prosecutor, comes through the door at a run and takes Huck to the ground. “You brought Zach here,” Ben says between blows. “He murdered their mother. He raped my wife.” It was a secret Charlie had kept even from him, and hearing it from him seemingly catches her off guard. “To see Ben ultimately in such fierce defense of her in that moment, I think that somewhere in her, that feels good,” Fahy says.

The camera goes to Sam and holds. Byrne says she is playing an older sister’s sense of responsibility in that close-up, one that has grown heavier since the loss of both parents. “Being the eldest sibling is actually a lot of pressure, and I do feel like Sam carries that with her every waking moment of her day,” she says. The memory of that night arrives with the close-up: two hooded men in the doorway, Gamma still chatting, a young Sam who has seen them first. Gamma, as evenly as she can, offers the intruders the $50 in her purse and $200 more from a mason jar if they will only leave.

Back in the present, Charlie makes a connection. “You called him brother,” she says. “I called everyone brother,” Huck says. For more than 20 years, that word pointed to Zach’s actual brother, Daniel, and Charlie will later say she is the reason he is dead. Ben has found the rest upstairs, a confession in Huck’s own hand: at 17, he had paid Zach $5,000 to kill Rusty on the night of the attack. Ben sneers that Huck lacked the nerve to do it himself and had to get a Culpepper.

Huck’s defense comes out in pieces. He admits he was the second man in the mask all those years ago, but the girls were supposed to be at track practice that day. He says he stopped Zach, and a flashback to the woods shows him turning his gun on his partner as Sam tells her sister to run; it goes off, and the bullet strikes Sam in the head. He pulled Zach off Charlie, then ran six miles to call his parents, who would not let him turn himself in.

Neither sister will hear it. Charlie says Zach chased her down like an animal. “He was the weapon that you loaded,” she says. Sam is colder; she tells Huck he should have hanged himself in the barn beside Annalie. Huck answers that he went to war, then came home to teach.

Then Charlie goes quiet. “She feels very angry at Huck and very vulnerable because they hooked up at the beginning and she didn’t know, and I think that makes her feel sick,” Fahy says. Sam takes over the questioning, driven by what Byrne calls “her fury at this man who’s still sort of begging for forgiveness.” Huck now has both sisters against him, uniting them “on the same team in a way that we haven’t seen yet,” Fahy says.

Slaughter gives Huck this much. “He was a very scared 17-year-old, and he did have a bad thing happen to him,” she says. “Now, it’s not a justification; it’s an explanation.” As for the lifetime of atonement he claims, she says viewers have only his word for it.

The secret Rusty kept for a decade

The rest of what Huck has to say is about Rusty. Sam already knows about the payments, $2,000 a month to Zach’s son so that Zach would never name his accomplice. Huck explains that his parents set them up after the attack, in a bargain brokered by the old Sheriff Coin, whose family still runs the law in Pikeville. Huck heard of it 10 years ago from his dying mother, and after her death he came to the farmhouse to confess. Rusty did not call the police, because he would not blow up his daughters’ lives with new trials, appeals and lawsuits. He made Huck hand over the money and took over the payments himself, then sat him down at the kitchen table to write a confession to the attack, the same pages Ben found upstairs that morning. Asked whether Rusty forgave him, Huck says no: Rusty called him one of two men on Earth he never would.

Rusty also told him why he held on to the confession. One day his daughters would have to decide whether to keep paying Zach’s family for Zach’s silence or give the confession to the police, and Rusty did not want the truth to reach them all at once. He put it in the words of an Emily Dickinson poem he and Gamma used to quote, and Sam finishes the line as her eyes fill with tears: the truth “must dazzle gradually.” “So it’s up to you now,” Huck says. “Both of you.” The scene cuts to squad-car lights pulsing blue in the dark. Huck is in handcuffs, arrested for now on a lesser charge: stealing the revolver used in the school shooting.

Slaughter says Rusty learned the truth when his daughters weren’t speaking. She also points to Charlie, who said on the night of the attack that she didn’t want anyone to know what Zach did to her. “I know from talking to survivors of assault that what they feel the loss of most is that sense of safety, and that sense that when they say ‘no,’ that will be honored,” Slaughter says. “I think it was really hard for Rusty to honor that, but he did, because that’s what Charlie wanted.”

Byrne says Sam finally understands how far her father went to protect Charlie. “I don’t know if she necessarily agreed, but I think he was between a rock and a hard place,” she says.

The price of being the good daughter

Nothing in Huck’s written confession mentions that Zach assaulted Charlie in the woods. So in the kitchen, while Sam deals with the police, Charlie asks Ben how he knew. Ben says Rusty told him shortly before he died, and called his agreement to stay silent the hardest decision he ever made. Charlie won’t let that stand. “It wasn’t a decision. It was a promise,” she says. “It was my secret.” Ben’s answer is gentle. “You only keep secrets when you’re ashamed. And he was never ashamed of you,” he says.

So Charlie tells him the rest. There was a miscarriage years ago, on a visit to Sam in New York, that she passed off as an infection. (She had three miscarriages in all.) She believes the assault is why she cannot carry a child to term, and she spent years punishing Ben for failing to guess. Ben asks whether a doctor ever told her so. None did. Then, to make her laugh, he lists his own humiliations, among them that he was the sole member of a Star Trek fan club, and tells her it doesn’t matter to him whether they can have children.

“The truth came out, and it’s only when that happens that I think she’s able to realize what keeping the secret did to her and to the people that she loved,” Fahy says. Now Charlie tells the truth, and “everyone’s still there to love her.”

Slaughter says the sisters had never really talked about what happened. “They’re hyper-articulate women, but they never say what they need to say,” she says.

They say it on the porch steps, where they finally settle what to do about the attack. Charlie wants to leave it alone, and Sam shows her that leaving it alone will be enough. Once the checks stop, Zach will talk. Sam tells her it really is that simple, as long as Charlie is out of Pikeville. It may be the first decision about that night the sisters have made together, and Charlie suspects their father planned it that way. She thinks he sent Sam to the farmhouse to look for an old photograph of Gamma, knowing the search would lead both of them to the record of the payments, and, eventually, Huck’s written confession. 

Until this week, Charlie had entrusted the truth about the woods to almost no one besides her father and Judith Pinkman (Paula Malcomson), who took her in on the night of the attack and now teaches at the school. Judith, it turns out, has been keeping a secret of her own.

A confession over a broken plate

The break in the school shooting comes when Sam has Ben bring up the school’s security footage and enlarge the gun until they can make out two arms around it, both in dark sleeves, one showing a sliver of a light shirt. Charlie remembers running into Judith, Doug Pinkman’s widow and Kelly’s after-school tutor, at the dry cleaner two days after the shooting, collecting the light shirt she had on when the shots were fired. Charlie goes to her alone and after dark, her phone recording, while Sam and Ben listen from a car outside. She is about to accuse the woman who sheltered her after the assault. “It’s another heartbreak for Charlie because Judith was there on the night, the worst night of her life,” says Fahy. 

Judith pours tea and asks for help mending a decorative plate, her grandmother’s, which has broken in half. She runs the glue along the edge and tells Charlie to press the halves together, then lays her own hands over Charlie’s. “Good girl,” Judith tells her.

The confession begins in the same even voice. Judith walked in on her husband, Doug, with Kelly in her classroom; Charlie supplies the legal term, statutory rape. When Kelly became pregnant, Doug called it God’s will and informed his wife that they would raise the baby and she would give up teaching. “Little by little, he just erased me,” Judith says. Slaughter says the betrayal went beyond the marriage itself, to Judith’s belief in “this system of marriage.” So Judith “trickled poison” into Kelly’s ear, convincing her that Doug meant to force her to end the pregnancy. On the day of the shooting, Kelly brought her father’s revolver to school and froze. “I stood behind her,” Judith says. “I wrapped my finger around hers, and I pulled the trigger.” Emma died when the two struggled over the weapon. Judith had planned to kill Kelly as well and step forward as the widow who stopped a shooter. “But I ran out of bullets,” she explains. 

Three times in The Good Daughter, Judith’s hands close over a younger pair. On the night of the attack, she held young Charlie’s hands under a faucet. At the school days earlier, she closed her own around Kelly’s on the gun. Now, at her kitchen table, she steadies Charlie’s on the plate. “Something is broken, and we’re going to put it back together,” Slaughter says of the mending. Sometimes, she adds, people don’t heal.

Judith knows she is being recorded on Charlie’s phone. When she has said enough, she loads a gun. Then she takes the phone and dictates a statement: she killed Douglas and Emma, and Kelly is innocent. Charlie pleads with her to keep talking. “This is my decision,” Judith says. She orders Charlie out. The door shuts between them. A shot sounds from inside, out of frame; Judith has turned the gun on herself. On the porch, Charlie collapses, stunned, and Ben reaches her. Sam and Charlie have started making their decisions together, but Judith makes hers alone, and it is final.

Five years for Kelly Wilson

Morning comes up over Pikeville in violet and pink, and Sam goes to the courthouse to make a deal for Kelly. Two Coins are waiting for her: District Attorney Ken Coin and the current Sheriff Coin. The district attorney concedes that Judith’s confession takes the death penalty off the table and calls any further leniency “gravy.” Sam starts listing what their offices got wrong with  the case. No one tested Judith’s hands for gunshot residue or took her shirt into evidence. Huck, who had talked Kelly into handing over the revolver, walked out of the school with it, and no one stopped him. Their deputy chief assaulted her sister in the school hallway. A school resource officer failed to notice a principal abusing a disabled student. Then she wonders aloud what she might find if she looked into the night Daniel died. It was a Coin, Keith, who shot Daniel, and the sisters have come to suspect the old sheriff planted the gun that made him look guilty. The Coins’ answer is to call her “honey” and remind her that her father loved this town. “My Daddy would tell you, fellas, that you’ve got two choices,” Sam says. “You can sign off on five years for Kelly Wilson or you can sh-t in both hands and start clapping.”

The line could have come out of Rusty’s mouth. Byrne says the case teaches Sam what she once held against her father: his “empathy for people, for all kinds of people, for the worst kinds of people.”

Five years is half of what Kelly receives in Slaughter’s novel, where she accepts a 10-year plea. The character has real-world roots: Kelly is loosely based on Jessie Misskelley Jr., one of the West Memphis Three, the Arkansas teenagers convicted of murder in 1994 and released in 2011 under plea deals. Misskelley, whose IQ was reported as 72, gave police a confession he quickly recanted. Slaughter studied what she calls his false confession while writing Kelly. “There’s a difference between reading something and seeing something,” says Slaughter, adding, “When you see her, 10 years seems like it’s too much, but five years seems fair.”

Kelly is less certain. Sam tells her that with good behavior she could be out before her baby starts school, and insists that the choice be hers. Kelly says “it seems like I ought to be punished.” “Does it seem fair to you?” she asks. Sam says it does, and smiles faintly as Kelly signs. Byrne doesn’t think Sam is as sure as she sounds. “It’s so tied into her own trauma and what she went through,” Byrne says. Sam “feels compromised by it,” even if it is the “best version of what she can get for her in that moment,” she adds. Kelly was used by two adults, and she is still the one going to prison. Slaughter hopes viewers ask “what does justice look like for them,” rather than what they would have done in the characters’ place. For Kelly, it looks like five years in prison and, for once, a decision no adult made for her.

The photograph Rusty hid

Kelly’s sentence is settled. What’s left of the episode belongs to the Quinns. Ben has job interviews lined up at Atlanta law firms, courtesy of Sam, and a question for Charlie: is she still his wife? “Yes,” she says. “Are you still my husband?” He is.

At Rusty’s farmhouse, the sisters and Lenore (Harper Steele), his longtime secretary, read through a box of his letters, including one meant for Gamma, with Charlie pulling faces at the intimate prose. Lenore remembers when one of them was written, because she had to bail Rusty out of jail. Charlie is moving to Atlanta with Ben, and she makes Sam an offer: When Sam is ready, she would like to hear more about Anton, the late partner Sam only recently told her about.

Slaughter did not want the moment to be purely sentimental. “It’s not some false candy-cane sort of get-together,” she says. “It’s giving each other a lot of crap and sitting around the table and bad-mouthing their parents.” The actors felt the ease in it. “It’s like the roadblocks were removed, and finally they could just see each other,” Fahy says. Byrne puts the change down to the truth Sam has finally been told. “She can finally understand what her sister has gone through, and it just shifts everything,” she says. “It’s like a tectonic kind of shift.”

They still haven’t found the photograph they’ve been looking for. Earlier in the season, Rusty told Sam about a picture of Gamma from their first date, a picnic because he couldn’t afford a restaurant, on a day when his heart felt like a kite and she was reeling in the string. He promised that Charlie would know where to find it. In the novel, Charlie comes across it only after Sam has gone back to New York, and emails the image to her. Here, they discover the photo at the same time, in the same place. “I felt it was important for them to find it together because the whole point of the emotional arc of the story is the sisters are separated and then they come back together,” Slaughter says.

By now, Charlie suspects there is no photograph, only a ruse to make them search the house as a pair. If the picture exists, she reasons, he left it in the open, like the rest of his secrets. “We need to stop thinking like he was Sherlock Holmes when he was barely Inspector Gadget,” she says. Then she asks why Sam has been carrying a framed photo of their mother in her purse. Rusty had asked her to bring it to the hospital. Sam turns the frame over and peels away the tape. Behind the first picture is the second. “I had forgotten how beautiful she was,” Sam says. “They were beautiful together,” Charlie says. Under the photograph is an envelope marked “Last word,” the sisters’ childhood way of claiming the end of an argument. Charlie says their father finally figured out how to use it.

As Sarah McLachlan’s “Long Road Home” rises, a love song about taking the long way back, a childhood memory swims into focus: tall grass, two girls lying beside their mother. Young Sam’s arm settles around young Charlie, and the camera climbs from the arm to their faces. Almost always, The Good Daughter has looked through one sister’s eyes at a time. This memory belongs to both. Then the frame widens on the grown sisters, still talking, the green country quiet around them.

The sisters take very different roads to that photograph. Charlie stayed in Pikeville, and spent more than 20 years avoiding what happened to her there. Fahy hopes viewers take something from watching her finally reckon with it. “When you face the things about yourself and about your past that hold you back, you open yourself up to the life that you want,” she says. Sam left for New York and stayed away. Asked what playing the character taught her, Byrne, who is Australian, points to the return. “I left Sydney, and I can relate to that,” she says. To her, “leaving your home and returning” is a tale “as old as time.”

It took both sisters to find the picture. Sam had it all along, sealed in a frame she carried to her father’s hospital bed and never thought to open, and it was Charlie, who thinks the way Rusty did, who knew to ask. Their father could not make his daughters tell each other the truth while he lived, but he could leave behind a confession that required them both to decide, and he could hide his happiest day where it would take them both to find. The finale that began on the farmhouse lawn, with a man telling the sisters what really happened on the worst night of their lives, ends at the same house with a snapshot taken before they were born, on a day no one in a mask ever touched, or ever could. For decades, Sam and Charlie kept separate accounts of what happened to them. They finish The Good Daughter side by side, two daughters with one photograph between them, agreeing at last on what they see.

title: A New Pill Could Reduce the Risk of Having a Second Stroke
content:
On November 9, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved a new type of medication to reduce the risk of strokes in certain populations.

Asundexian, which will be sold under the brand name Sunharbo, is a daily pill that is the first to target a specific factor in the blood-clotting process that can contribute to stroke. In a study submitted to the FDA by Bayer, researchers found that the drug, when combined with an antiplatelet therapy such as aspirin, reduced the risk of an additional stroke by 26% in just over a year compared to people who received placebo and the antiplatelet therapy. The drug is approved for people who have recently had an ischemic stroke, which occur when clots block blood flow to the brain, or a transient ischemic attack caused by a temporary blockage of blood flow to the brain that doesn’t cause permanent damage.

“The data is quite robust, and the feedback from the international stroke community is positive,” says Dr. Ashkan Shoamanesh, professor of medicine at McMaster University, who co-led the trial. “We’re eager to have this on hand as soon as possible for patients.”

There are two types of strokes: ischemic strokes, caused by blockages in the blood vessels, can impede blood flow to critical organs including the brain, and hemorrhagic strokes, caused by weakened blood vessels that burst in the brain and cause excessive bleeding. About 87% of strokes in the U.S. are ischemic.

Each year, about 795,000 people in the U.S. have a stroke, and nearly one in four strokes occur in people who have previously had one. Recurrent strokes represent an unmet treatment challenge, says Shoamanesh. But treating ischemic strokes requires using just enough clot-breaking—or blood thinning—medications to dissolve the blockage without causing excessive bleeding. Asundexian appears to do just that. The 26% reduction in stroke risk occurred without any significant increase in bleeding events, according to Bayer’s data. “We used to always have a challenging balancing act,” says Shoamanesh. “Here we have the major benefits without the bleeding risk, so there is a large amount of excitement.”

Researchers have known for years that some people born with a genetically driven lower risk of stroke have lower levels of a compound involved in blood clotting, called Factor XIa, in their blood. It's a minor contributor to forming clots when the body experiences a major bleeding trauma like an injury, but it plays a bigger role in smaller vessel ruptures, some of which can contribute to stroke, says Shoamanesh.

It took more than a decade for scientists to turn that observation into a viable medication, says Dr. Christoph Koenen, chief medical officer at Bayer. But asundexian prevents small clots that may form in the vessels from becoming larger ones that can grow to block blood flow. One of the findings that most impressed the researchers was that "it didn’t matter how old people were, from what part of the world, what their medical history was, or what type of ischemic stroke they had—all of the patients seem to benefit similarly from the treatment,” says Shoamanesh.

Given the encouraging results in reducing the risk of recurrent strokes, Koenen says Bayer is exploring "if there are other benefits of asundexian we can bring to different patient populations.”

Asundexian will be available starting in November. Shoamanesh expects that in order to truly benefit from the drug, patients will have to take the daily pills for the rest of their lives. Data that tracked some of the study participants for several more years showed that those on the drug continued to show lower risk of stroke compared to those taking placebo. “That means that the drug continued to provide an advantage even at later time points,” he says. “So we expect this to be a lifelong drug based on the data. And we expect this will be the new standard of care.”

title: The Unexpected History of 'Black Friday'
content:
Since the 1950s, Black Friday—once simply known as "the day after Thanksgiving"—has grown into a quasi-holiday in the United States marked by steep discounts, ceaseless shopping, and occasional violence. But more recently, Black Friday has also metastasized. It's not a day anymore. It's a week, a month, a veritable state of mind. (Speaking of which, check out Lifehacker's Black Friday coverage. We got all the deals, baby!)

While pre-dawn trips to the mall are waning as online shopping grows, in-person shopping on Black Friday is still a big deal in the U.S.—it’s estimated that around 80 million Americans visited a brick-and-mortar store on Black Friday in 2025. But how did Black Friday come about, and what does it all mean?

When was the first Black Friday?

“Black Friday” in the United States originally referred to the start of the Panic of 1869, when the collapse of the price of gold devastated the national economy. “Black Friday” as a description of the day after Thanksgiving dates back to 1951; the term first appeared in the journal Factory Management and Maintenance, where it referred to the number of employees who skipped work on the day after Thanksgiving. Around the same time, the police in Philadelphia and Rochester started informally using “Black Friday” to describe the traffic and crowds that appeared in their cities as shoppers hit the stores on the day after Thanksgiving. The phrase gradually caught on. It was picked up by national press in 1975 when the New York Times used "Black Friday" specifically to describe the day after Thanksgiving and the shopping and sales it brings.

But even before it had a name, Black Friday was a thing. The day after Thanksgiving has been known by merchants as the start of the shopping season since the late 1800s. By the early 20th century, retailers sponsored Thanksgiving Day parades that traditionally ended with an appearance by Santa Claus, as if to say, “Now it’s time to shop for Christmas.” By unspoken agreement among retailers, Christmas-themed advertisements rarely appeared before Thanksgiving in our grandparents’ day. This informal bargain obviously no longer applies.

Black Friday’s problematic name

Referring to a day as “black” traditionally denotes a period of calamity or tragedy, leading some to suggest different names for the day. In the early 1960s, Philadelphia merchants suggested “Big Friday,” a name which did not catch on, leaving retailers with the weak explanation that the “black” in Black Friday refers to the black ink denoting profits in a ledger. Oft-repeated lore suggests that retailers are "in the red" all year, and only start making an annual profit at the end of the year, but big retail chains generally make money all year long.

A more modern issue with the name is that Black Friday sales now last for days or even weeks, beginning in early to mid-November and bleeding over into the following Saturday, Sunday, “Cyber Monday,” Tuesday, and beyond, leading people to say things like, “Do you want to go Black Friday shopping this Sunday?” So far, alternative names like “Five-Day Frenzy” and “The day I get to trample someone to save $8 on a Nespresso” haven’t caught on. But here’s hoping.

The failure of “Black Thursday”

Beginning around 2010, an insatiable thirst for profits led many retailers to push the start of Black Friday shopping to Thursday (aka Thanksgiving Day). Kmart opened Thanksgiving morning. Toys R Us opened that night. By 2011, Walmart was opening its doors at 10 p.m. on Thursday. The trend led to widespread backlash, with many Americans appalled that employees were forced to work on Thanksgiving or angry that consumerism was encroaching upon a holiday meant to celebrate colonialism. By 2021, most major retailers had relented and elected to remain closed on Thanksgiving.

Cyber Monday is Black Friday’s accidental offspring

The term “Cyber Monday” describes the boost in online retail sales on the Monday after Thanksgiving, sparked by workers returning to the office and getting right to online shopping. The term first appeared on Nov. 28, 2005, in a Shop.org press release entitled “'Cyber Monday’ Quickly Becoming One of the Biggest Online Shopping Days of the Year," which may be the most influential press release ever written. Since its early 2000s birth, Cyber Monday has become the biggest online shopping day of the year. Americans spent $14.25 billion online on Cyber Monday 2025, according to Adobe Analytics. So is Cyber Monday bigger than Black Friday? Retailers really don't care: Analysts now tend to mash everything into the category of "Black Friday–Cyber Monday" (or even "Cyber Week").

"Buy Nothing Day" is the inverse of Black Friday

If all this naked consumerism makes you a little squeamish, you're not alone. Anti-consumerists have named the day after Thanksgiving “Buy Nothing Day,” which you can celebrate by doing charity work, cutting up your credit cards, or simply not purchasing anything. Pioneered by artist Ted Dave and popularized by Adbusters magazine, the first Buy Nothing Day was celebrated in Canada in 1992.

It’s hard to measure the success of the alternative holiday. Both online and brick-and-mortar retail sales have increased sharply since 1992, suggesting Buy Nothing Day’s effect is negligible. On the other hand, maybe big retailers are losing millions because someone on Bluesky reminded you not to shop. Sure.

How many deaths has Black Friday caused?

Depending on how you measure it, Black Friday has resulted in between one and 17 deaths. Jdimytai Damour is the only person killed directly due to a Black Friday sale: The 34-year-old worker was trampled to death by a surging crowd at a Long Island Walmart on Black Friday in 2008. If you include car accidents, shootings, retail worker suicides, and fatal heart attacks, Black Friday’s death toll balloons to 17, with 128 reported injuries.

Black Friday violence has even inspired a horror flick: Eli Roth's 2023 holiday-themed slasher Thanksgiving opens with a hilariously brutal Black Friday riot at a big box store, setting off a chain of events that involve a lot of people being murdered by a dude in a Pilgrim mask.

Is Black Friday just hype?

I mean, yeah, of course. Critics of Black Friday point out that there are arguably better times to buy a new TV (like the week before the Super Bowl), not to mention plenty of other goods. Savings from Black Friday shopping are often illusory—big-ticket “doorbuster” items generally sell out quickly, leaving behind goods that are, by and large, priced the same as they would be at any other time of year. Some retailers even mark up products ahead of Black Friday so the discounts look bigger. If you're buying online, your browser history, location, and cart contents can tweak the prices you see on Black Friday, as they can on any other day.

Yet despite protest holidays, the unpleasantness of shopping when stores are overcrowded, and the frustration of hunting for bargains that often aren't that great to begin with, Black Friday stubbornly remains an unofficial holiday, celebrated by over 100 million Americans in one way or another. What that says about our country's relationship with capitalism is unclear, but personally, I’m going to continue my own day-after-Thanksgiving tradition of eating pie for breakfast and thinking about going for a walk, but then watching The Quick and the Dead instead. I'm not protesting anything; I just don't need the hassle.

title: Five Things I Wish I'd Known Before Getting a Foldable Phone
content:
We may earn a commission from links on this page.

The iPhone Duo might be the highest profile foldable phone to date, but it’s by no means the first. Personally, I’ve had my eye on the Google variant, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold—and recently I finally took the plunge. I thought I’d done my research to know how different having a foldable phone would be, but I still had a bit to learn. Here are some of the things I wish I’ve learned along the way after making the jump to foldables.

The aspect ratio matters a lot

One of the most notable aspects of the iPhone Duo is how wide its screen is, even while closed. And there’s a good reason for that: The larger screen while open has exactly the same 1.41:1 aspect ratio as the smaller screen while closed. This has a ripple effect on how every app you use looks and feels—and whether you like Apple’s approach is largely a matter of personal preference.

Compare with my Pixel 11 Pro Fold, which features an extremely tall 2.17:1 aspect ratio when closed, but a nearly square 1:04:1 aspect ratio when open. On the outer screen, apps are a little less wide than on my old phone, but there’s plenty of space for reading books or articles on the inner screen.

I like the tall, thin display personally because it feels easier to reach buttons with my thumb, and the wider display is better for reading. However, this approach can occasionally result in some odd app layouts. Not every app is designed for tablets, especially on Android, and shifting the aspect ratio between the inner and outer display sometimes means re-rendering or even restarting an app entirely to load properly.

The iPhone Duo has a more consistent aspect ratio and general feel between the inner and outer display, but it comes at the cost of a really wide phone. Neither approach is better or worse on its own, but it might be worth going to a local store to get your hands on the phone you’re thinking about before buying.

The inside screen scratches more easily

For years, the screens on most smartphones have been made of increasingly tough and scratch-resistant glass. So tough that you might not even need a screen protector anymore. On a foldable phone, that can be true of the outside display, but it’s very much not when it comes to the inner, foldable display.

Screens might be foldable, but the strong, durable glass that makes your phone so scratch-resistant isn’t. No matter what foldable phone you use, the covering on the inner display will be more flexible, and thus softer. Apple uses a nano-texture polymer film that can be replaced, but the film on most foldable phones cannot. That means if they get damaged or scratched, those marks will be there for the life of your phone.

If you (like me) haven’t considered a screen protector in a while, it might be time to try one again, at least for the inner display. It’s also worth keeping in mind how rough you plan to be with your phone. Construction sites or factories might not be the best home for a foldable phone you plan to open a lot, but an office job should be a bit safer.

The case situation can be weird

Similar to the screen protector issue, cases can be more of a headache. Most rigid cases will come in two pieces, and the piece that covers the outer display can be shockingly minimal—barely more than a frame, for some of the cases I looked at. A poorly made case can be brittle or pop off more easily, so it’s more important to get a high-quality one.

If you like to use your phone case as your wallet, it’s also important to be wary of cases that aren’t specifically designed for your model of phone (and maybe some that are). A lot of wallet cases are built to unfold to reveal your phone’s screen on one side, and your cards and ID on the other. But depending on how your foldable phone unfolds, it could be awkward to reach the inner screen.

The hinge also introduces more spaces for dust and debris to get into your phone. Despite the extra moving parts and gaps, most foldable phones still offer the now-standard IP68 dust and water resistance rating. That mainly applies to what can get inside and damage the components inside your phone. It’s still possible for hair and dirt to get gummed up in any pinchable spaces, so look out for any case that might provide even more nooks for dust to collect in.

Give all your apps' settings a second look

I’ve set up most of my apps how I like them by now, but when I first got my foldable phone, I had to revisit some settings I thought I was done messing with. One of the most notable examples was my ebook apps: I was previously using a single-column, medium-font layout, but it looked ridiculous on the inner display. After switching to a two-column layout, it not only felt more natural, but a lot like reading a regular book.

Similarly, there were some uses for my calendar app that got a whole lot more useful. I’ve never really been able to use anything other than either the one-day or Schedule view if I want to make out anything, but on the inner screen, I can finally look at my week at a glance. But that meant tweaking some things—like showing reminders, which fit naturally amid my events in Schedule view, but become a cluttered mess when I saw 14 different reminders to take my meds at once in the Week view.

Most apps do a decent job of automatically adjusting to different screen sizes, but I found a few outliers that I had to figure out myself. As an example, Google Docs would default to a view with extremely tiny text when I first started using it. It took me a bit to figure out that this was due to a “Print layout” toggle in the document’s settings. This is, for some reason, enabled by default when opening a document on the larger inner screen. It can take some time to learn the eccentricities of all your apps, but it’s worth poking around when you can.

Don’t forget about the outer screen

I know, it sounds so obvious, right? The outer screen is the one you’ll use most often, so how could you forget about it? But when you unfold the inner screen, the outer one is still useful in some surprising ways that I hadn’t even considered until I went poking around in some of my apps.

One of the most adorable examples is the Made You Look feature in the Pixel’s Camera app. When unfolded, you can take a picture using the rear camera and see a preview like normal, while the outer screen shows silly animations to capture the attention of a baby or toddler that you want to look into the camera. Admittedly, this is an older feature, but it’s a clever one. For adults, you can also use the outer display to get a selfie preview while using the rear-facing camera.

The outer screen is also just better for some things. YouTube is one of the few apps that has a unique layout designed for a partially folded screen, with the video playing on the tilted-up portion of the screen, and video controls on the bottom portion. 

However, in my experience, it was a lot nicer to watch a YouTube video by just propping up the outer screen by unfolding the phone a bit, like a kickstand. My Pixel even detected when YouTube was in full-screen mode on the outer display and would be more forgiving of unfolding the phone without switching to the inner screen. The phone anticipated I might just want to prop up the smaller screen, which I thought was a nice touch.

title: The Next Chapter of mRNA
content:
It’s been a very good year for Stéphane Bancel. On a crisp October day, the CEO of Moderna, of COVID-vaccine fame, is sitting in his glass-walled office in the company’s headquarters in Cambridge, Mass., weeks before encouraging results from the company’s first mRNA cancer vaccine would become public. He’s recounting the biotech’s rocky road turning an unproven, scientifically dismissed approach—using messenger RNA, or mRNA, the genetic code that instructs cells to make proteins—into a platform for producing new categories of medicines.

Fifteen years ago, Bancel had his doubts. At the time, there were no approved mRNA-based products on the market, and most scientists would have agreed that mRNA was too unstable to form the basis of a new class of medical treatments. In fact, the entire biotech industry had bet—successfully—on manipulating another, more reliable genetic material: DNA.

“It was crazy to think of using mRNA as a drug,” Bancel reflects. But that was before a fateful meeting forced him to look at the genetic material in a different way, and realize that with the right manipulation, mRNA provided a way to make drugs that were never possible with existing strategies. Now, he believes that nearly any protein drug made today with existing, recombinant DNA technology can also be made using mRNA.

The company’s goal isn’t to follow the usual road map and make one type of drug for one disease at a time, but to build a new platform from which a variety of different treatments can be developed in a plug-and-play scenario—similar to how the computer-technology industry is built on the foundational hardware and operating systems around which a whole universe of software has blossomed. “mRNA is the information molecule, so if you find the way to safely and effectively get it into the right cells, you can unlock a lot of medicines to help people’s suffering,” says Bancel.

Moderna’s mRNA COVID vaccine saved an estimated 2 million lives globally—while earning the company $46 billion—from 2021 to 2024. This fall, people are getting its newly approved mRNA flu shot, the first of its kind. And in October, Moderna announced with Merck that their mRNA approach also worked to stimulate the immune system to fight cancer—creating a therapeutic vaccine, rather than a preventative one. Intismeran, combined with one of Merck’s drugs, successfully kept melanoma from recurring in a group of patients with mid- to late-stage disease. By the end of the year, Bancel says, he expects to unveil similarly encouraging results from Moderna’s first mRNA therapy for a rare disease.

In just over a decade, mRNA has gone from molecular misfit to biomedical golden child, in no small part because of Bancel’s efforts at Moderna to prove the naysayers wrong. “At the beginning, it was either zero drugs, or we find a way to climb this mRNA mountain and make a lot of drugs,” says Bancel. 

Consider vaccines, where mRNA is quickly becoming the preferred technology for its speed. Scientists at Moderna can create a vaccine against any pathogen within six to eight weeks—far faster than it takes to then conduct the human studies required by regulatory agencies to establish a therapy’s safety and efficacy. Cancer researchers hope to harness that speed with customized mRNA vaccines like intismeran.

That’s what Bancel saw in mRNA more than a decade ago: an untapped vein of therapeutic ore. With mRNA, once it’s properly instructed to make the right proteins to fight a virus, fix a genetic disease, or tackle a tumor, the human body becomes its own treatment factory.

Over a series of interviews with TIME spanning several years, Bancel unveiled the story of how a startup betting on an untested technology came to sit at the same table as decades-old pharmaceutical giants, and now holds the key to a transformative platform that could redesign treatments in three critical areas: infectious diseases, rare diseases, and cancer.

Born in Marseilles, Bancel grew up with a strong interest in math and science, fueled in part by his father, an engineer who was always fixing things around the house. “We used to sail in the summer, and one summer my brother and father and I sailed from Marseilles to Mallorca—a two-day trip—and the engine broke in the middle of the water in the middle of the night,” he says. “I remember we were holding the flashlight above him, and he was fixing the engine by himself.”

Bancel was pursuing a degree in chemical engineering at Ecole Centrale Paris when, on a whim, he took a genetics class at the university next door and “fell in love with genetics,” he says. He went on to earn a master’s in chemical engineering at the University of Minnesota and an M.B.A. from Harvard Business School before working at Eli Lilly in Indianapolis for six years, mostly in manufacturing.

In 2006, he became CEO of the French diagnostics company bioMérieux. He was working in the company’s Boston office in 2011 when he got a call from his friend Noubar Afeyan, founder of Flagship Pioneering, a venture-capital firm and health-startup incubator. Bancel served on the boards of several of Afeyan’s startups and had already turned down multiple offers to lead some of the new companies. But Afeyan thought he finally had one that might entice his friend.

Afeyan had been approached by a trio of scientists with the idea for a company to develop new treatments from mRNA. He showed Bancel data from a handful of mice that had been injected with human mRNA to make a human protein. “I’m like, ‘This is impossible, because everything we learned in biology is that if you inject mRNA, you create an immune response,’” says Bancel. But what if it worked? Afeyan persisted. What would it mean? “I said, if it works, you’re going to be able to make hundreds, maybe thousands of medicines that you cannot using [current] biotech technology,” says Bancel. 

Up to that point, the biotech industry was focused on manipulating DNA and making products to work on molecules that cells secreted—all in cell cultures using bacteria or viruses that were genetically engineered to produce the molecule in question. mRNA, on the other hand, works inside of cells, temporarily adding new genetic instructions for the cells to make new proteins, which could replace missing ones in certain diseases. In the case of infectious diseases or cancer, it could theoretically make proteins to stimulate the immune system.

But mRNA was too unstable to turn into a treatment formulation and too aggravating to the immune system, so the possibility of mRNA generating a new class of drugs hadn’t advanced past “what if.” When Bancel asked his good friends from college and business school whether he should take Afeyan’s offer to helm the new company, everyone told him “Don’t do it,” he says. Two other biotechs—CureVac and BioNTech (which would become Moderna’s competitor during COVID), both from Germany—had a head start on exploiting mRNA. But Afeyan was convinced that Moderna could lead this new field. Bancel had a choice to make, Afeyan said: Flagship would proceed with the company, with Bancel either as its head, a board member, or a regret-filled bystander. 

The chance to build something in biotech from the ground up and figure it out along the way proved too tempting for the engineer in Bancel. In 2011, the company went from being called LS18—short for Life Sciences 18 in Flagship’s ledger of startups—to Moderna, a mash-up of “modified RNA,” with Bancel as its first CEO.

Bancel had experience in the pharmaceutical industry, but he had no playbook for starting a new company based on an unproven technology. He dived straight into every aspect of the company—even getting on the floor to build secondhand desks himself at Moderna’s first headquarters in Cambridge—and pushed himself and his team hard. “The key was, how do you get to that one drug before you run out of money and investors throw in the towel on you, saying we’re done?” he says.

Moderna spent its first few years in stealth mode, with no website, to the point that media and market watchers called the company suspiciously secretive. Analogies were drawn to another startup: the blood-diagnostic company Theranos, which was equally private about its product and ultimately turned out to be fraudulent. At the time, Bancel shrugged off the comparison, saying he didn’t want the world to watch Moderna’s teenage years, as the company developed the technology he was convinced would change medicine.

“My wife Brenda in those first two years thought I was clinically bipolar,” says Bancel. “I would come home some days so energized by the work; I would lie in bed not sleeping because my head was spinning, thinking all night because I was so excited. Literally three weeks later, I would come home borderline depressed, thinking, ‘Sh-t, this is never going to work.’ Brenda would ask, ‘Which is it? Is it going to work or not work?’ I said, ‘I don’t know. Nobody in the world knows, because it’s something that’s never been done before.’”

What inspired Bancel to keep going was the magic trick of viruses, which could essentially do what Moderna was trying to do: introduce new genetic information into a cell and thus co-opt it to make a specific protein. “If you look at nature and learn from nature that it’s possible, then your willingness and your appetite to invest capital is much stronger,” he says. “That’s why I tell my engineers, ‘Yes you can—you just don’t know how yet.’”

There were two big hurdles with turning mRNA into drugs. One was finding a way to control the immune response it generated, and the other was finding a way to deliver the mRNA to the right cells. Both tasks fell to Antonin de Fougerolles, Moderna’s first chief scientific officer, and his team. De Fougerolles didn’t have much to go on. “It’s like blank sheets of paper,” he says. “Eight or nine out of the 10 experiments aren’t going to work. Startups always have a lot of pressure, but I would put Moderna on the high end of that scale in terms of pressure.”

“It’s a very hard place to work,” Bancel acknowledges of the intense environment to produce results. “We debate and debate,” he says. “Every voice makes the discussion better. But it’s not for everyone.”

Early on, with input from his team, Bancel decided to focus Moderna’s limited resources on rare diseases involving missing proteins, because seeing if the mRNA could replace them would be a relatively quicker process.

Dr. Stephen Hoge, an emergency-room physician turned health care consultant at McKinsey, arrived at Moderna in 2012 to help the company prioritize specific disease areas. Hoge liked what he saw during his months at the company and accepted the board’s invitation to join, eventually becoming president in 2015. “I think of him as a brother from another mother,” says Bancel. “If he tells me we need to jump out the window -because it’s good for Moderna, I would jump with him, and on the way down I would ask, ‘Why are we jumping?’” The two often hold contrasting points of view, leading to legendary debates that both see as key to Moderna’s success. “Stéphane and I have argued through the entire history of the company,” says Hoge. “And we often joke that if one of us takes one side, then the other has to take the other. But it’s been part of our success that we often disagree to find the truth in between.” Hoge championed using mRNA in cancer, but also approved a side project exploring how mRNA could work in a vaccine for infectious diseases. It made sense that the drawback that had led many to dismiss mRNA as a treatment—its aggressive stimulation of the immune response—could be an advantage in a vaccine. The first impressive results showed that all of the mice inoculated with the mRNA flu shot had high levels of antibodies to fight influenza weeks after being challenged with high doses of the virus, while the unvaccinated mice did not. The results were exciting enough to add a more robust program on infectious-disease vaccines to Moderna’s port-folio, which would later form the foundation of the company’s COVID vaccine.

One day in 2015, Dr. Tal Zaks, Moderna’s chief medical officer at the time, stuck his head into Bancel’s office with his typical greeting: “Hey, boss.” Zaks had been tracking Moderna’s work in developing vaccines against infectious diseases, and knew the progress the company was making represented an advance over previous efforts—including his own failed attempt at developing a breast-cancer vaccine while a postdoc at the National Cancer Institute. But researchers were also understanding the important role of T cells from the immune system in recognizing cells that had been infected by viruses and were producing viral proteins—in a way similar to how cancer cells make foreign molecules. “One thing we learned along the way in cancer immunology is that it’s very hard to cure cancer without the immune system,” says Zaks. Advances in immunotherapy—including with checkpoint inhibitors, which unleash the body’s immune cells on cancer—could complement an mRNA-based cancer therapy. “All the strands were coming together,” he says, for a potentially successful cancer vaccine.

“He said, ‘I think we should do a cancer vaccine that is individualized because we can sequence for cheap now the healthy cell and the cancer cell from a biopsy, and we can make an mRNA coding just for the mutations in the cancer,’” Bancel remembers Zaks telling him. “‘We can inject it and combine it with a checkpoint inhibitor, and I think it has a very high chance of working.’ And that was the first day I thought about the idea of intismeran.”

Zaks was up-front in reminding Bancel that no cancer vaccine to that point had worked, and that the idea would require an expensive randomized controlled trial that would cost Moderna more than any study it had ever conducted. “If we were going to do this, we would need the technical capability to do it at scale, creating a personalized vaccine for each person,” Zaks says he told Bancel and the Moderna board. “If we couldn’t do that, it wasn’t worth the effort.” Zaks proposed focusing on melanoma, which has many mutations for immune cells to target, and also advocated testing patients earlier in their disease, to see if the mRNA therapy would reduce the risk of the cancer returning.

Bancel and the board were in. To fund the program, Bancel reached out to Merck, which makes pembrolizumab (Keytruda), a checkpoint inhibitor. Bancel had already invested in a manufacturing facility in Norwood, Mass., about 45 minutes from the company’s headquarters, that would ultimately take on the work that had started in -Cambridge—sequencing patients’ tumors, generating the right mRNA codes for their vaccines, and then making those vaccines, all under one roof. The Norwood facility would eventually be the hub for making many of Moderna’s products, while manufacturing for intismeran shifted to a new facility in Marlborough, Mass., in 2025

“Given that this experiment was so bloody expensive, it had to have a ‘wow’ effect size,” says Zaks, who is now a partner at global investment firm Orbi-Med. “It couldn’t be on the margins. So we had to do the smallest trial we could do and still show this really whopping effect size so it was not questionable.”

Figuring out how to find the red flags on tumors (the markers distinguishing cancer cells from normal ones), and which ones to target with mRNA to get the best response, was critical. “I figured that we needed to code in a very deterministic fashion because we needed a robust process that was replicable,” Zaks says. He asked his sequencing team the maximum length of mRNA messages they could make, and Zaks added his own knowledge of how long mRNA sequences for tumor markers needed to be; “the rest is simple math,” he says. The ultimate number of those tumor red flags that Zaks and his team settled on was 34—the number included in intismeran. “It was no magic number that we calculated somehow with complicated math,” he says. “It was extremely simple—what length of mRNA did we need to make it reliable, and how long did we need to make each one to cover what tumors expressed? To date, in 2026, this is the only strategy [in cancer vaccines] known to work.”

Just as patients were enrolling in the study and the Norwood facility was starting to make the mRNA cancer vaccines, Moderna and the world were hit with an unprecedented health emergency: COVID.

Bancel saw an opportunity to put the power of mRNA to the test and decided to pivot nearly all of the small company’s resources to developing and manufacturing a vaccine against the SARS-CoV-2 virus. He had reason to be confident. By 2020, Moderna had already conducted eight clinical trials involving mRNA shots against various viruses, from influenza to cytomegalovirus (a common and chronic herpes virus) and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). In early human studies, all eight vaccines had generated good antibodies against the viruses in question. But, says Hoge, it wasn’t immediately obvious that the pandemic would become a long-term public-health threat, and he and Bancel debated Bancel’s decision to almost completely divert the small company’s resources to the pandemic effort. “‘Do you want me to stop treating people with cancer? Do I turn away a melanoma patient?’” Hoge remembers saying. “In the end, both of us ended up being right or wrong, depending on your perspective.”

“I love the fact that the first mRNA COVID vaccine was made in the intismeran manufacturing facility,” says Hoge. “But we didn’t build Norwood for cancer or infectious diseases or rare diseases. We built it for all three. People ask, How could such a small company be ready for the COVID pandemic? We weren’t. We had a platform that allowed it to happen.”

Hoge says that “COVID, without a doubt, catapulted us forward,” referring both to the tremendous real-time knowledge the team gained while developing the first mRNA vaccine against SARS-CoV-2, as well as the worldwide validation of the safety and efficacy of the approach that might have otherwise taken a decade or more. It also put Moderna on the map.

Even while being diverted to produce billions of doses of the COVID vaccine, the cancer-vaccine program continued to enroll patients. This October, almost a decade after starting development on an mRNA cancer vaccine, Moderna and Merck reported the “whopping effect” that Zaks had hoped for. Intismeran, combined with pembrolizumab, reduced the recurrence of cancer by 42% in people with mid- to late-stage melanoma. And the benefit, as Zaks had predicted, started to emerge after six months of treatment. “The immune system takes time to be activated,” says Dr. David Berman, chief development officer at Moderna.

Beth Ryzyk heard the promising results while watching the news. In 2024, after being diagnosed with Stage IIIC melanoma, Ryzyk had decided to join the study of intismeran at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSK). Surgeons removed her tumor as well as the lymph nodes under her arms, and after genetic sequencing, she learned she had 80 tumor markers. In the study, Moderna and Merck focused on the markers they thought would trigger the strongest immune response and designed a personalized vaccine for each of the patients in the treatment group. “It’s pretty amazing that they can individualize it to me and teach my body what to fight,” she says. The treatment is straight-forward enough that she received the intismeran and Keytruda near her home at MSK’s location in Westchester, New York. She still doesn’t know if she received the vaccine or a placebo, since the study has not been published yet, but she gets scans four times a year. Two years later, “so far so good—nothing has popped up, and it’s the best I can ask for,” she says. “The hard thing about melanoma is that it can come back to any part of your body, and it’s always in the back of your mind. So if it prevents 42% [of recurrence], I’ll take that.”

Bancel and Moderna are no longer alone in seeing the promise of mRNA, especially as part of the emerging group of immunotherapies for cancer. They have been joined by a chorus of researchers eager to capitalize on turning patients into their own treatment factories, with an assist from mRNA. They envision a future in which cancers are detected and treated with immune-based approaches like mRNA vaccines that can change the trajectory of cancer—bending the progression curve back down. “If we can increase the proportion of patients who have surgery and treatment [with an mRNA vaccine], then fewer patients with Stage IV melanoma will exist,” says Dr. -Michael Postow, chief of the melanoma service at MSK, who enrolled patients in the intismeran trial. “We could turn this disease into something where we exclusively prevent all recurrent melanoma, and that would be a wonderful place to be—although clearly we are not there yet.”

Bancel anticipates filing for U.S. Food and Drug Administration approval soon, with a possible decision on intismeran in 2027, but he isn’t waiting to explore other cancers for which the vaccine might also show benefit. Moderna is currently conducting nine clinical trials involving intismeran in melanoma, kidney, gastric, lung, and pancreatic cancer, as well as an early-phase study testing it alone, without a checkpoint inhibitor, in Stage I lung cancer.

Earlier this year, the National Cancer Institute launched a $200 million fundraising initiative to support mRNA cancer-vaccine trials, and in 2024, MSK created the Olayan Center for Cancer Vaccines to make personalized mRNA vaccines like intismeran from start to finish—beginning with genetically sequencing patients’ tumors, to generating the mRNA sequences targeting their cancer, to working with manufacturers to make the vaccine, to administering them. (The James P. Allison Institute at MD Anderson Cancer Center in Houston, where checkpoint inhibitors were discovered, is planning to launch a similar center.) It’s an opportunity to push development of next-generation vaccines by taking risks on new approaches that biotech and pharma companies are not as comfortable with. “We want to add on to what industry is already doing, and at the same time innovate and test futuristic versions of mRNA cancer vaccines that academic centers are more suited to developing and testing,” says Dr. Vinod Balachandran, head of MSK’s new center. “It’s an exciting time for cancer vaccinology.”

Future refinements will include exploring whether the personalized approach of designing vaccines for each patient is truly scalable and affordable. One of the advantages of mRNA is that it doesn’t require growing cells but relies instead on computing power to analyze and generate the right mRNA sequences to target each patient’s cancer. “No cell cultures need to be grown,” says Berman. Traditionally, bespoke approaches have not been practical as treatments, because of the time and cost required to custom-design therapies. But Berman “absolutely” believes an mRNA platform can uniquely address both the time and potential cost of customized treatments. “We have scaled down the technical footprint and have plans to scale up [the program] to look at different tumors,” he says.

While Moderna benefited from the unexpected revenues from the COVID vaccine, those profits, and growing concerns among the public about mRNA technology and vaccines more broadly, made Bancel and the company targets. During the pandemic, Bancel was criticized for earning a huge raise and benefiting from exercising stock options granted in 2013, while many countries were unable to secure enough doses of the COVID vaccine to protect their populations. Bancel says he donated nearly all of his increased -earnings to charity, including through one he and his wife launched, Bancel Philanthropies, and created mRNA Access, a program for bringing Moderna’s expertise in making mRNA vaccines to academic and public-health groups in the developing world without the high cost of licensing fees.

Then came the second Trump Administration. During President Trump’s first term, mRNA was given equal footing with more traditional vaccine-making approaches because of the urgency of the pandemic, but in Trump’s second term, mRNA became technology non grata. Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Secretary of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), is a longtime skeptic of vaccines, including ones involving mRNA. In 2025, scientists reported being confidentially advised by staff at the National Institutes of Health (NIH), which reports to HHS, to avoid using “mRNA” in research-grant proposals if they wanted to be successful in securing funding. Conspiracy theories about permanent genetic manipulation resulting from Moderna’s and Pfizer-BioNTech’s mRNA vaccines—not based on any scientific evidence—flooded the internet, and more people distrusted the technology.

In May 2025, HHS canceled a $766 million contract with Moderna to develop vaccines against pandemic influenza and bird flu. In a conversation the following month at Moderna’s Norwood facility, Bancel said he remained committed to mRNA technology, despite significant headwinds from the Administration. “The vision has not changed,” he said then. “It’s science, and you always have to start with the science. I don’t know how to do anything else. You can say it doesn’t exist, and you can fight it, but gravity is gravity—and I believe the same is true with biology.”

Bancel eventually secured funding from the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations, the group that funded part of Moderna’s early COVID-vaccine development, after pledging 20% of production of a future approved vaccine to low- and middle-income countries, and began Phase III testing of its bird-flu vaccine in October 2026.

The company’s first mRNA vaccine for seasonal flu was on its way to being reviewed by the FDA when Bancel received a letter in early 2026 stating that the agency refused to review the application, finding fault with the way the trial was designed, despite having previously discussed and accepted the study. The government ultimately reversed its decision and approved the mRNA flu shot in August 2026.

But the drop in revenues from waning interest in the COVID shot and the canceled government contract were a brutal blow to Moderna’s financial health, and Bancel was forced to lay off 10% of his workforce and shut down or delay some projects. “Business-wise it was easy, because you do the math, but emotionally it was really hard to separate with people who helped us build the company,” says Bancel. He also made difficult decisions to terminate some projects, including one for developing a vaccine against cytomegalovirus, which had been the company’s leading candidate before COVID.

Then came the encouraging results on intismeran. Bancel hopes the latest findings lay the groundwork for a rich pipeline of cancer treatments to come. He’s realistic enough, however, to know that the biotech ride is a roller coaster. Weeks before Moderna’s encouraging news, the company’s competitor in the mRNA space, BioNTech, reported that its mRNA vaccine failed to show any benefit compared with placebo in a similar combination with a checkpoint inhibitor among patients with advanced head and neck cancer. Experts say that the two companies use different approaches in developing their vaccines and that BioNTech tested its vaccine in people with later-stage cancer that could not be surgically removed, while Moderna chose to intervene earlier, making it difficult to compare the two.

The conflicting results are not unusual with a new technology, and Bancel is even more convinced than he was in 2011, back in Afeyan’s office, that mRNA is the technology of the future and will generate hundreds of new treatments for a range of diseases. By the end of the year, he expects to announce late-stage results from the first mRNA treatment for a rare disease in which people are missing a key protein that processes other proteins and fats.

“I always think about the long cycle,” says Bancel. “I knew that if you can figure out the engineering puzzle of building a business with mRNA, then the impact of this technology on humanity—way after I’m CEO, way after I’m dead—is going to be gigantic. And we are just beginning. We are just getting started.”
